utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. We must ask you to finish within the hour, given the constraints of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may have to abandon a lot of material. I shall do so. I have planned on that basis. Mr. Lilic, there will be many points where I shall be asking you for yes/no answers; I hope you will be able to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 469, tab 24, is the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 4th of October, 1998. You've reviewed this when preparing to give your evidence. In it, we find Perisic arguing that a NATO strike is unavoidable, Djukanovic stating that he is opposed to war, and suggesting that everything should be done in accordance with the United Nations Security Council resolution. Milutinovic and the accused make statements consistent with one another. What was your inference from the fact that they made statements consistent with one another, please, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very particular record of minutes that was being kept at a time of great danger for the FRY, and there must have been a prior meeting at which this overall situation was reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minutes provides alternatives --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I need on that. We'll move on to paragraph 194 in the summary, bringing the exhibit back, please. Was there a meeting of the Kosovo staff coordinated by Milutinovic on the 13th of June of 1998, attended by a large number of political and military elite, including, apart from Milutinovic, Pavle Bulatovic, Perisic, Dimitrijevic, Samardzic, Pavkovic, Stojiljkovic, Djordjevic, Sreten Lukic, Sainovic, Stanisic, Obrad Stevanovic and possibly Minic, the accused not being present?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of the debate, what did -- paragraph 198 -- what about Stojiljkovic say in relation to the one and a half million Kosovo Albanians in Kosovo? What was your reaction to his observation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I must briefly explain that that meeting follows on to a visit that occurred prior to that in Djakovica where Mr. Stanisic reported on the overall security situation in Kosovo and Metohija and on the behaviour of certain reserve police units. So at this meeting, that same discussion was continued, and I cautioned Mr. Stojiljkovic regarding what was going on at Kosovo and Metohija, particularly around the village of Ponasevac, to which he responded very strongly. We had a heated dialogue, and he said, in the final analysis, they should all be killed, but he was irritated by what I had said. And I said that because of what certain members of the reserve police force were doing, one day, we might be ashamed for being Serbs and our children will be ashamed and the children of our children will be ashamed. And I asked Milutinovic to intervene in response to this outburst.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 199, line 3, did the purpose of this meeting apparently have something to do with participation of the army in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conviction is that that meeting was intended in the first place to analyse the overall situation in Kosovo and Metohija primarily from the security point of view. Secondly, to examine the behaviour of the army top leadership, which did not wish to accept acting in coordination with the police. And thirdly, to show that Mr. Stanisic was not conducting the operations in Kosovo and Metohija properly in view of the fact that he was insisting on a unity of command and more efficient activities, particularly in the centres of terrorist activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 200, was there a meeting following that, a narrower meeting, where it was decided to form a particular body?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting on the 13th was the only meeting of its kind that I attended, upon the proposal of Mr. Milosevic in the first place. But according to my knowledge, there was a narrower meeting after that when it was decided to form the united command of the state security and public security forces of the police, and the command of those forces was given to Mr. Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Lukic's appointment said what of Stanisic's authority?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that shortly after that, Mr. Stanisic was withdrawn from Kosovo and Metohija and transferred to Belgrade, so his command position was taken away from him with respect to the state security. Immediately after that, a couple of months later, Mr. Stanisic was replaced from his position altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will see a reference in the summary to an existing exhibit which I won't weary us with today, Exhibit 319, tab 9, which dates from a little earlier, the 15th of May of 1998. The witness has reviewed this document, which was signed by Djordjevic and related to the formation of a staff in the ministry at Pristina. And at that earlier stage was the body formed in Pristina, Mr. Lilic, a national security, not a joint command body?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that order signed by Mr. Djordjevic, the head of the public security service, it relates to the public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 202, there was a decision to form a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism. Tab 25. If we can just briefly look at that. Very briefly. And you can see the composition of this ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism, Lukic, Gajic, Djinovic, Lukovic, Trajkovic, Radosavljevic, Vukovic, Zdravkovic and Vucurevic. Is this joint security forces, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was signed by Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic, Minister of Internal Affairs. This is the unified staff of the public and state security services, including special units. One can see that Sreten Lukic is at its head, and there is a mixture of people from state security and public security. Gajic is from state security, Milorad Lukovic is a member of the special unit but he belongs to the state security, and so on. But some of the people I don't know personally, but that is the staff as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. This was previously tendered through Babovic as 466, tab 6. 466, tab 6, I am told. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've covered already the changes in the rules of the Supreme Defence Council. We can see them considered at tab 26, just for reference, in the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council for the 23rd of March of 1999, and the witness has already commented on the coincidence of that date in relation to the NATO bombing. We don't need to look at it beyond that. It can be exhibited, I hope, by my referring to it in that way. Just tell us this, please, Mr. Lilic: The new rules changed certain previous arrangements. They no longer allowed for telephone consultation and they included the requirement that the Federal Ministry of Defence and the chief of the general staff must be present at sessions. In your judgement, what did that say - paragraph 209 of your summary - what did that say of the move of responsibility, if any, for what was to follow from the accused?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, that's something that used to be the practice in the previous Defence Council is now being formalised and made obligatory. So I think it also implies the corresponding sharing of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So as a result of this, there would be less responsibility on the accused? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to say that he would have less responsibility, but there was a possibility for certain decisions not being taken if the provisions of the new rules of procedure are not respected. So possibly it was possible for certain decisions not to be taken if taken in accordance with the rules, that is, through the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 210: The witness has reviewed a previous exhibit, Exhibit 245, instructions for the defence of inhabited places. I'm not going to present that again to the Chamber. You've reviewed this instructions for the defence of inhabited places. Are you able to form a view, Mr. Lilic, as to whether that comes from the existing defence plan?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document that I managed to see, the source of which I cannot know, certainly is part of the country's defence plan adopted by the Supreme Defence Council, the implementation of which is determined by the Supreme Commander, and I must say I was surprised to see it in this form without the accompanying decision of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 215: Did you, Mr. Lilic, shortly after the start of the NATO bombing campaign, hold discussions with various foreign officials, including Frans Vranitsky, Moammer Ghadhafi, and Helmut Kohl? Were these discussions held with the knowledge of and, as you understood it, with the approval of the accused, and did they lead to your writing a letter to the accused on the 5th of May of 1999, tab 27?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the beginning of the bombing, or some 15 days into it, it was clear that the raids would not last, as had been expected by a certain number of people in the Yugoslav leadership, so I tried my best to use connections and influential people that I had met earlier on, and my answer to your question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sure you understand that the detail of what you would be saying is contained in your summary so that people can know the detail if they need to pursue it and it's just simply for the pressure of time that I would ask you to be brief. Am I right in the question that I asked you, that you had these international discussions and wrote the letter concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to finish my sentence, and I was going to say yes, anyway, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at this letter, which sets out your cogently expressed arguments in favour of the Kohl plan - and the learned Judges can consider it in detail later - it ends on what is page 4 of the English text at the foot and simply the end of letter. It ends with your saying to the accused that: "The responsibility of each one of us is historic. Perhaps we experience it differently." And you indeed conclude by saying that: "The fate of the Serbian people, the fate of Serbia and the FRY, is in your hands." Now, did this draw any reaction from the accused himself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding what is stated in this letter, prompted by the wish to make an attempt to stop the bombing, no. As far as my personal status and the attitude towards me is concerned, it provoked a very tumultuous reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 218 of the summary: Were you called to a meeting with Milutinovic, Marjanovic, Tomic, Jovanovic, Minic, at the Presidency of Serbia's building on the 17th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this effectively a party hearing, or as you describe it, a party tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that those were people who were the leaders of state institutions and political bodies in the SDS, it was like a political and state tribunal which acted in that way with respect to the letter we referred to. It was literally a trial for something that they themselves did not understand and in which they themselves had not participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the particular complaint against you, in a sentence, was what?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I shouldn't have given myself the liberty to write such a letter to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a concern as to how such a letter might be interpreted or subsequently used as evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was quite openly stated by Mr. Milutinovic, though that is something that really never occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 28, did you write a further letter to the accused on the 17th of May? Again, the Chamber will be able to review it at leisure, Mr. Lilic, so we can deal with it in a sentence. Did this reject the criticisms made of you and did it end, as we can see on the second page, the penultimate paragraph, your asserting your desire to help without personal interests and your willingness to step down after the aggression was concluded?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the following months, months that followed these events, did it become clear to you that one of the political or military options was being favoured? If so, which one?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite clear that as far as the attitude towards NATO was concerned, the conviction was that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could even have some influence; at least, some people believed that NATO could be defeated, and this was later stated in certain public statements, to break the spine of NATO, as people said. So I really do believe that those were unreasonable beliefs, and that every effort should have been made to stop the bombing as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 222 of the summary, Perisic, Stanisic, and Dimitrijevic were all replaced or sideways moved. Do you believe there to be a link between those moves and the accused's wife's JUL Party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm convinced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 224, Perisic was replaced by Ojdanic. I think he was somebody who you yourself had actually relieved of command, is that right, or moved from one post to another as your judgements on the man?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From position of commander of the 1st army, he was moved to the general staff, which was a position that was higher - I think he was deputy chief of staff - but it had marginal powers, insignificant powers, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 29, please. We can see how this matter was dealt with at the Supreme Defence Council meeting held on November the 14th of 1998. Page 3 of the English, under "Personnel Issues," and at the top right-hand corner for you, Mr. Lilic, 2465, is the page number, it's the bottom of the page where the session is opened with the accused reminding of the necessity to replace the chief of the general staff because it was said he had been on duty for a long time. If we look further on, we see about a page further on that President Djukanovic of Montenegro expressed a contrary view. Milutinovic, on our page 4 of 3, it says -- it says concurred with the views of the accused. And then at our page 5 of 3, as it's recorded, Djukanovic's response was that "the Supreme Council of Defence is working the way it does. If you agree with that, then it will be that way. I am against." So there was a conflict. You can see it all in detail, if necessary. Any comments on that conflict between Milutinovic and the accused and Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think that such an important issue should have been resolved by a consensus, and in the new rules, such a provision is made with regard to such a high position in the army of Yugoslavia. Secondly, it is really not important how long somebody's doing a certain job, but how he's doing it. And thirdly, regardless of the fact that the president of the Republic of Montenegro, Mr. Djukanovic, had a very firm position, the decision was nevertheless taken by Milutinovic, who concurred with President Milosevic and gave legitimacy to a decision which in those days, according to the rules in force, could have been taken by Milosevic alone without any polemics. But it is a fact that the chief of staff was always appointed and dismissed with the absolute concurrence of both Republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're recorded as saying the decision was taken by Milutinovic. Did you mean Milutinovic or Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milutinovic agreed that Perisic should be replaced. And by agreeing, in a sense, he made the decision. But the final decision is made by President Milosevic, who confirmed it with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 226, what's your understanding or belief as to the reason why Stanisic was relieved of his command and replaced?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yesterday we spoke at some length about the principled positions of Mr. Stanisic, when it came to the struggle against terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija regarding the need to have the public security under a single command, the need for the army to provide logistics, but in a legitimate way, and I think that was one of the reasons. But no less important reason was the fact that it didn't suit the Yugoslav left. And immediately after that, the story was spread about that Mr. Stanisic was working for the GSYA, and this was rumoured for quite a long time until he was dismissed. It is true that Mr. Dojic [phoen], the director of the GSYA was in Belgrade, and he spoke with a different person, and he had a tete-a-tete meeting of more than four hours with somebody quite different, but I don't want to go into that now. The point was for the Yugoslav left to have its people take over the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Dimitrijevic, did you regard Farkas as up to the job? Paragraph 227.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without underestimating General Geza Farkas, I don't think that he was somebody who could have replaced General Dimitrijevic, not only for professional reasons but for certain other reasons as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 228, the failure to call a state of emergency resulted in what, so far as responsibility falling on Milutinovic was concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that a state of emergency was not proclaimed has as its consequence the illegal and unlawful deployment of the army of Yugoslavia, and quite certainly, that somebody's responsibility ought to be sought, and not only Mr. Milutinovic's as far as the Republic of Serbia is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, the failure to call a state of emergency was the decision of whom?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a decision, a possible decision, made by the president of Serbia possibly. But under conditions of that kind, it ought to have been a decision by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia because it implied the use and deployment of the army of Yugoslavia, or rather, the Supreme Defence Council, their decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 229, voting on the Rambouillet accords was in which Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I think it was the Assembly -- the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that proper or improper, and if improper, what does that show of the accused? What does that reveal of the accused's method of operation, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think that the fact that the National Assembly discussed proposals and positions to be advocated at Rambouillet is its legitimate right. However, at the same time, it was the duty of the Federal Assembly to discuss issues of that kind as well. So this kind of responsibility is left at the level of the Republic of Serbia and marginalises the federal state in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just dealing generally with the composition of those assemblies, party composition gave authority to which party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, de facto, the SPS was the party mentioned everywhere, at all levels, but the SPS was not the party that covered the most important regions of power, but my answer would be the SPS at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just remind us, we covered it in detail, but just to have a general, would it be the case that the president of Serbia when he was only the president of Serbia or was the president of Serbia, the accused was able to control federal institutions? How did he achieve that? By what method?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we're talking about Mr. Milosevic's -- if that's who you have in mind, I think his influence should be viewed from two aspects, one from the aspect of a head of state, and the authority vested in him throughout those years. And secondly, as a leader of the political party, first of one, then the other, and then both. So it was via the political parties, in fact, the SPS and JUL, that this influence was dominant, by the deputies in the Federal Assembly or via the deputies in the Republican Assembly or rather the ministries in either government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, paragraph 230, you were shown or listened to, rather, an audio recording. The number is given on the summary. We have nothing like the time to go through it. It's audio recording T0000114. You heard the recording in preparation for evidence. Whose voices did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the tape, there are a number of voices. I was able to recognise just one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the voice of General Mladic, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's at tab 30, Your Honours. And now I must sweep up matters that were postponed yesterday on grounds of possible sensitivity, but I think there's no need for any closed session. A couple of matters of detail, please. Can you have tab 17 in front of you. This shows the termination of professional military service for Galic, General, whom you're aware has been on trial here. And we see your signing off on his termination. Can you just explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that I signed this document because this isn't a decree that is specific for decrees of the Supreme Defence Council, which I presided over, and I don't know this Colonel Branko Fezer either. But I don't think that's of any importance. Now as far as signing this decree, the members of the 30th cadre's centre, I think that I spoke about this a great deal yesterday. We didn't view the personal centre and the individuals in it individually, but we looked at the people who had belonged to the JNA or who on a volunteer basis were on the territory of Republika Srpska. This decree probably came as a proposal by Mr. Radovan Karadzic, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Now I want to turn to another topic. Yesterday you volunteered to us in relation to Srebrenica that certain individuals were responsible. Can you tell us, please, who those individuals were.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult that you can expect me to name any individual. That would be difficult. I don't think you can expect me to do that. But I think that there is individual responsibility, and I am sure that in the course of this trial, you will be able to show and prove who those individuals were. And I said I was convinced that that kind of order didn't come from any political or military person from Belgrade, and that I'm completely sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, that's the third time you've told us that. Can you help us please, because time is very short, with this: You volunteered that individuals were involved. Can you just perhaps help us with who it was.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Had we known who was involved, we would have taken the appropriate measures ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How soon after the massacre at Srebrenica were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to be precise enough. I think it was a relatively short space of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Days, weeks, days?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. How soon was the name of General Mladic, who, of course, is indicted in respect of Srebrenica, associated with those events publicly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of polemics and discussion as to that. According to the intensity of President Milosevic's anger, the degree to which he was angry, I don't think much time elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now go to tab 20, please, Your Honour. And I'm going to ask that you add to tab 20 so that it becomes part of it an earlier record of the same general kind. Tab 20 at the moment is the 29th of August, 1995, Dobanovci meeting. The one that you're now being provided with is the immediate preceding one is the meeting of the 25th of August. And Mr. Lilic, I'd be grateful if you would take, please, the B/C/S version which has page numbers in the top right-hand corner, small page numbers, at least starting on page 2 it does, and I will guide you to the relevant passage that I want you to look at. Starting at the beginning, this is a record of a meeting of the highest political and military leaders on the 25th of August in Dobanovci. And it's in accordance with conclusions adopted at the 42nd session of the Supreme Council held on the 23rd of August of 1995. Can you help us, please, with this: Did General Mladic attend Supreme Defence Council meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic was invited in his capacity of a man who can exert pressure on the leadership of Republika Srpska to accept the groundwork and basis to prepare the peace negotiations in Dayton. So my answer is yes, he was present at the initial stages of the Supreme Defence Council meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go then please to English page 4, at the foot, and for you, Mr. Lilic, I think it is page 6 at the top. Now, this is not a Supreme Defence Council meeting, it's a special meeting following on the SDC meeting, and we see the following at the foot of page 4: "Since General Ratko Mladic arrived at the meeting at about 1430 hours, President Milosevic addressed those present and instructed them that this meeting is secret, that is, it can never be mentioned or referred to publicly, and he quoted a letter that President Karadzic sent him on the 23rd of August, saying that the letter entailed 'important elements.'" Was the proclamation of secrecy linked to Mladic's arrival, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see following on from that, President Milosevic reminded him, reminded Karadzic that he suggested that...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Reminded Karadzic, "he suggested that very thing a year ago. The Muslims had to be offered something they deemed important, and they would give us something we would be particularly interested in. Of course, we're not referring to the enclaves. The three in Eastern Bosnia (Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde) would blend into Serbian surroundings without a fight." Was that the general view of the Serb leadership at the time, please, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but may I be allowed to put you right on one point, or rather a detail in this document is not correct. The letter received by President Milosevic from President Karadzic, and the response to your question is no. My answer to your question is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Further down, page 5 in the English, and at the very foot of page 6 for you, Mr. Lilic, we see at the end of the paragraph, two-thirds of the way down, the accused saying: "... Under-Secretary of State Holbrooke told him about the U.S. view according to which, if the Serbs fail to accept the peace, the war would be made to escalate. And if the Muslims refuse the peace solution they will be told they are to be left alone with the sword of Damocles hanging above them in the form of General Mladic." Was that the approach taken by the Serb leadership to the use of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that from the text you can see, according to the words of Mr. Milosevic, that this was stated by Mr. Holbrooke.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over the page, please, to our page 7, and for you, please, Mr. Lilic, your page 8. A quarter of the way down in the English version, Prime Minister Kontic "informed the others that the economic situation in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had been increasingly difficult and that we would not be able to assist Republika Srpska as we have been so far. When President Karadzic heard about this inability to assist Republika Srpska, he asked President Milosevic, 'President, does this mean that I shouldn't go to the Neretva and into Eastern Slavonia?' The President of Serbia replied that what Karadzic was suggesting was a war option." Do you remember that passage of debate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember that debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move on, please, because I'm going to come to your contribution to this debate in a second or so. But at the foot of our page 7, we have Karadzic warning that the Muslims aspire towards all the territories west of Brcko and are prepared to leave the Drina area east of Bosnia "to us. Therefore, we must fight for a wider corridor and as compact a territory as possible..." Is that the policy being accepted and discussed at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's clear that as broad a corridor as possible was needed at Brcko. As for the agreement and common position, this was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your contribution can be found on English page 9, B/C/S page 11. This is what you said: "[President Lilic] stated that the question of whether we are giving up on Krajina is now moot. We have done everything to help Krajina, but what happened happened. They left their traditional homesteads without a fight. You could rather say that the Krajina politicians have given up on their mother country. [The accused] added a less-well-known piece of information. Namely, he mentioned a telegram sent to General Mrksic in which he was told to hold out for just two days until we send him help. They did not hold on. They fled." You, Mr. Lilic, continued, stating that "the key question at the moment was whether we would keep, whether we would retain Republika Srpska or not. The question of Serbian destiny is now posed." You went a step further than the previous speaker by saying that "for us the issue of a quick war or a quick peace practically no longer exists. Now we must only choose the quick peace" solution; and as the chairman of the Supreme Defence Council, you warned that "military resources are fairly exhausted, that some are depleted. That is why we are making a historical decision today: Will Republika Srpska exist or not. It will if we accept peace, not war." Is that your attitude?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over the page to page 10, we see the contribution of General Mladic. It's at your page 12 at the top. And in the middle of the page, I haven't the time to read all of it out, but just point it to the Chamber. It was Mladic expressing his satisfaction at seeing all Serbian politicians gathered since, as he said, "This is no time for a tug-of-war competition." Is that the reality of General Mladic's contributions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the specific way this sentence rang, yes, I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No discussion recorded here on Srebrenica. Was the topic raised at the meeting, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this meeting was related to the Dayton peace agreements exclusively. Of course, Srebrenica was discussed before that, before the meeting, as to what was actually going on, but for their part, there were no explanations or recognitions of any kind, confessions or such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Mladic give any explanation? Was he challenged by anyone?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mladic arrived -- No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has Mladic ever given you an explanation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You speak to Mladic, do you, from time to time, or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When most recently?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our intensive conversations took place precisely after these meetings, or to be more specific, in December sometime when I went with General Perisic and Dimitrijevic to make an attempt to save the French pilots, and this was a condition posed for the signing of the Dayton agreement in Paris. And we had intensive conversations at that time, and negotiations at Han Pijesak because President Milosevic, at my initiative, had accepted the fact that I should go to Han Pijesak where I talked at the time to practically the whole of the main staff of the army of Republika Srpska. And after very difficult discussions and debates, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just yes or no: Mladic never explained Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The personnel centre continued to pay Mladic until when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to Mladic himself, but to the whole group, the personnel centre paid out the salaries until 1994. This afterwards, social and welfare and assistance, and as far as I know, this went on to the year 2001, up until March. Whether Mladic was paid out as well, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there ever any investigation to your knowledge by the SDC of what was being alleged about Srebrenica? Was there ever any decision to cease supporting any of the VRS soldiers possibly implicated in that event?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next part of the similar record, as I'm very short of time. It's the other part of tab 20, and it's the record for the 29th of August, 1995. Just look at two excerpts on this, please. And in the English version at the bottom right-hand corner, the page numbering is 6 of 19. Mladic is present at this meeting as well, as we can see. But on page 6 of 19, which in your case, Mr. Lilic, can be found on page 5 at the top right, we have Karadzic saying: "We ought to insist on having Serbian territories compact --" sorry. "We ought to insist on having Serbian territories compact, answered President Milosevic. Let us leave Gorazde, Muslims alone would offer it on exchange." Is that an expression or view that the accused offered?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this, but as I know the principled positions with respect to the exchanges, then I think yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the foot of the English page and just a paragraph or so on, we have the accused warning again there wasn't much time left, "that it was in our interest to reach an agreement, for if we fail to do so - neither Republic of Srpska would exist, nor its Constitution." Was that the fear you all had?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is enormous pressure, and from President Milosevic, too, to go to the Dayton negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At page 8 of 19 in the English, and at page 11 for Mr. Lilic, we see the beginning of -- we see Mladic's contribution. I don't have time to go through it for want of time. So far as the 30th personnel centre is concerned, can you remember, please, we know that there was an embargo against RS between August 1994 and sometime in 1995. When did the 30th personnel centre actually resume paying salaries, please? What part of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the position taken by General Mladic, which he presented on the 10th, or rather, 11th of December while I was in Republika Srpska at Han Pijesak myself, to abolish the borders on the Drina, then I assume that that did not even take place in 1995. Perhaps at the beginning of 1996, but the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was so exhausted by that time that I don't think it was able to finance this at the rate that it had been able to do previously, the monthly sums that were paid out, and I spoke about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that the resumption of payments was in 1995, and you dealt with the matter in preparation for giving evidence, and we can find the paragraph number. What are you saying as to when the salaries were paid in 1995, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me to say, after the sanctions were introduced against Republika Srpska, we took a decision that the minimal part, that is the social welfare part, should be given to the families of the 30th personnel centre to continue their children's education, and I think that part of it was continued. That's what I had in mind. But they were not the entire amounts, they were just amounts that were guaranteed -- salaries guaranteed in the Federal Republic at that time, the guaranteed wages in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in what part of 1995 did those payments resume, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those payments were hardly interrupted, this minimum guaranteed portion, for a part of the members of the personnel centre who were mostly threatened. And I think those lists exist today and you can have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You shall be asked some further questions. Oh, one other question I should have asked you: You remained a member of the SPS until when, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-August 2002, I was replaced. I was given my work booklet and was left without a job in the state administration. And then I tabled my resignation to all the other posts that I held in the SPS, et cetera and other volunteer ones within the Federal state. So it was until mid-August 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 2000, not 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll deal at the end of the evidence with the tabs that haven't been produced. By and large they're SDC records outside the period of this witness, it obviously being of only limited value to have his comments on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a query about tab 8, if we've dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 8 is currently marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 8 is one that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 8 is one that the government representative are now happy that I should deal with because it falls outside the narrower period for which they would otherwise want protection. In those circumstances, may it now be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The other matter is the confusion between 466, tab 6, and our own 469, tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm told that the other exhibit is different from this because it's only an extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And therefore, since it was an extract upon which a witness may have relied for his views and opinions, it's probably preferable that it remain as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, I just want to take you back to an early part of your testimony, the 1997 runoff for the elections. You were the SPS candidate, and I believe you said that the campaign was obstructed by the JUL, and Mira Markovic, and that their influence affected your position. Could you tell me or let me know whether anything was done, any strategy, specific strategy was employed by them to affect your campaign? You eventually withdrew your candidature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson. This entire campaign was obstructed in terms of the media, including the fact that information from my election campaign and rallies were broadcast towards the end of the evening news. And the TV was in our hands, so to speak. I'm speaking from a political point of view, from the point of view of the political party. And it's another thing that I found out later on, that even the actual ballot counting was influenced. But by your leave, I really would not like to discuss that particular subject here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I start cross-examining this witness, I would like to hear your position concerning the time that I have available. As you can see, Mr. Nice just gleaned through certain documents. He just asked the witness to identify them. Quite simply, we have a pile of documents here that had merely been identified, and nobody went into their substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, we've got to bear in mind that the amicus may have some questions. We have to bear in mind that there may be some re-examination. But subject to that, you can have the balance of the time until the conclusion tomorrow. But in this case, in particular, I counsel you and warn you not to waste time arguing with the witness - if you do, the time will be taken against you - or to deal with irrelevant matters. Now, we'll see how we get on. We'll see what progress we make. But that is the time at the moment that you have available.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means until the end of the day tomorrow? That is just somewhat longer, a bit longer, just a bit longer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the way in which your time is taken up, arguing. Now, move on. Ask the questions. And I suggest you begin with the tabs about which there could be no dispute. There may be dispute about the admissibility of other questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to be efficient, Mr. May, I will try to move in some kind of order, taking the same order, perhaps, that the examination-in-chief took. I think that would be appropriate, and we are going to get to the documents, too. But before that, just a few questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The subjects that are being discussed here are Kosovo, Bosnia, Croatia. In view of information offices held familiarity with the situation, to which extent did the Serb people, the Muslims, the Roma, the Turks, Egyptians, the Gorani and others, and other non-Albanian population in Kosovo, to what extent were jeopardised in Kosovo by the Albanian Separatist Movement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the members of these ethnic groups that you mentioned were equally jeopardised, I would say, and it is certainly their survival in Kosovo and Metohija were jeopardised and any kind of safety and security, including their economic safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Economic safety is very important, but this is something more important than economic safety and security, and that is life jeopardy, vital jeopardy. So what extent were they vitally jeopardised? To what extent were their lives in danger in view of the constant killings that were going on in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a short while ago as number one that their safety and security was truly jeopardised and yes, their lives were in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the fact that there were many killings, Mr. Nice put the question as to whether I knew about that. I think that this is a bit of a misunderstanding between you. I don't think you understood each other correctly. You spoke about a large number of killings whose victims were primarily Serbs and other non-Albanian population and the perpetrators were Albanian terrorists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be seen from the transcript. I was very precise. I said there was a very large number of attacks by Albanian terrorists. It goes without saying that they were not attacking themselves. They were attacking the Serb and other non-Albanian population. But they even attacked the Albanian population in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That would have been my next question. Is it correct that there was a large number of Albanians who wanted to live in peace, who wanted to live in cooperation, tolerance, and who had very good and friendly relations, and that they were also victims of the Albanian separatist forces, especially the Albanian terrorists?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are very precise reports to that effect, and I think that these Albanians were a great force that we should have drawn on in terms of improving the relations between Serbs and Albanians. These prominent Albanians who were prepared to have this kind of coexistence in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did this ever happen in our policy, or rather I am referring to the time period when you and I were in the political -- on the political scene. I'm not talking about before that. Was there ever a single moment when a distinction was not made between the terrorists of the separatist movement on the one hand and the Albanian people on the other hand? I don't know if I have been clear enough in putting this question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to wait for the interpreters because I don't want to make their life too difficult. It's clear enough. If you're talking about this period until 1998, when in some cases there were some uncontrolled operations. I talked about that, but that is really an exception. So this was an answer to your question. There were no such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we never identified Albanians terrorists with the Albanian people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for uncontrolled behaviour or rather, crimes, that you referred to and that happened, did all officials know, political officials, police officials, and military officials, that no operations should be launched if civilians were to be imperilled by that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a clear, principled stand that was often highlighted. I was not often present at meetings after 1998, but I know about the period when I attended these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So my categorical position is that even as far as operations against terrorists are concerned, these operations cannot be launched if civilians lives would be jeopardised. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the position that for each and every crime, the perpetrators should be held accountable and that not a single crime should be concealed regardless of whether it is a question of looting, theft, or the most serious crimes, like killings, rape, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that position, but we also presented different examples, and we sought investigations and we wanted to have this matter looked into. But whether it was carried through, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Generally speaking, since a sufficient number of documents have been introduced here, I would nevertheless like to bring in another one which shows what our political position was precisely in mid-1998. I have a tape recording here of the 16th session of the main committee of the Socialist Party of Serbia. At the end, there are even the minutes and also the press release that was subsequently issued. In the minutes, it says that the persons present -- that the meeting was attended by Slobodan Milosevic, president of the Socialist Party of Serbia, and then the vice-presidents who were present. I don't want to use too much time, and among these vice-presidents was Zoran Lilic, and so on and so forth. This is the 16th session held on the 10th of June, 1998. So that is when the problem in Kosovo had truly escalated. Now, I want to ask you the following: Do you remember this? I'm going to quote only part of what I said in my final remarks. I am quoting this, and I am putting a question in advance. Do you remember this position? This is a meeting, a session of the top party leadership. There is a list of all the attendants. There is a couple of hundred of people, and also presidents of the municipal committees. That is in the meeting room where we usually had about 400 people present at such big party meetings? Is that right? So do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you have to answer this, Mr. Lilic, you can have a look at the minutes. The accused can read out the passage he wants to rely on, and then you can have a look at the minutes yourself. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I ask for a copy at some stage because it's not a document we have immediately available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let us have it here. We'll have it in evidence in due course. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You'll receive it. I have just one copy. I have no reason why not to give you the entire minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this passage that refers only to the item on the agenda that involved the debate on Kosovo, do you remember when I spoke about that, this is what I said: "Our policy is that Kosovo should be resolved by political means. We approach this solution bearing in mind our convictions, our programme which involves the principle of national equality -- ethnic equality. We don't want to harm the Albanians in any way, and we do not want Albanians in Kosovo to be second-rate citizens. Therefore, we should bear in mind, as Minic pointed out in his report, because he did submit a report in this regard, we should bear in mind, therefore, that we should make a major distinction, and we have highlighted this several times, between the separatist movement on the one hand, and the Albanian people on the other hand, the Albanian people who live there. No matter what this looks like," I mean, I'm skipping over certain passages because I want to save time but you can have a look at the entire text. "No matter what this looks like, this is precisely the approach that we should espouse. A political solution and also promoting the principle of ethnic equality. We should also bear in mind that those who have been manipulated," because, beforehand, I said that some Albanians, some people had been manipulated and some of our comrades said that the majority was manipulated. So we should bear in mind that even those who have been manipulated should be taken into account. "These are unfortunate people who are being manipulated like all the pauperised masses in the world. And it is these world manipulators who are trying to use them in order to destabilise southern Europe. And in this way, they are trying to create an alibi all the time in order to have a military presence of the great powers. They are not the mainstays of activity." I am referring to the Albanians. "They are being used by someone as their vehicles." Here it says Fukoshi, but I am actually referring to Bukoshi, so it's a typo. He became a millionaire in Germany, collecting funds allegedly for the needs of the Albanians, and so on and so forth. And then I conclude by saying: "In relation to Kosovo, a political approach, in relation to Kosovo the principle of ethnic equality. As for our political activity down there in Kosovo, not only our personnel in Kosovo, but also our people outside Kosovo who should be down there." And then I say: "Dialogue." You may remember that I spoke at the end, and I extemporised, I didn't have a written speech, but I hope that I have been consistent enough. The dialogue that started, I am referring to the dialogue when Rugova was there and so on and so forth. "The dialogue that began is not reserved only for the state commission and for the representatives of Albanian political parties, for Ratko Markovic, as you recall, this was the Deputy Prime Minister who led the government delegation there, and Mahmut Bakalli, or Bajazit Nushi, and Gani. This dialogue is not reserved only for them. Of course, it is not only a Serbian/Albanian dialogue, but it is also a Serb/Albanian/Turk/Muslim/Roma/Montenegrin dialogue, everybody should be involved. This dialogue should be present at all levels in the municipality, at local commune level, in a formal and informal sense. Formal and informal dialogue because people should be mobilised for life itself." And then I say that: "There is a clear difference in terms of where the terrorists are operating as opposed to places where there is a normal and peaceful life. They see this. And I think that all sensible people do not want to see destruction, misery, suffering of the civilian population. Everything that this process may bring forth. So on the one hand, we are going to insist on dialogue. And we are going to work for a political solution. On the other hand, we have to deal with terrorism. If the Albanians themselves manage to halt terrorism, good for them. We wish them all the best in this endeavour." Again, I'm skipping passages. And then I move on to say: "The party should coordinate political activities down there," so I emphasised that. "Political activity. That is the role of the party. Milo Martic, Dusko Matkovic, Minic is in charge of this three-man team for coordination on behalf of the party leadership of political events down there in Kosovo." So I hope you remember this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see those minutes. Would you mark the passage or indicate somewhere the passage you've relied on so that he can check that. Yes, if the usher would collect them, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give the whole minutes to the witness, and he can look at page 52, the passages that I have marked, begins with Kosovo to the end. And I've marked what I have quoted. But I'm quite sure that the witness remembers very well that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are tape recordings, I assume, from the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a transcript of the tape recording.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. May, I do indeed remember this meeting very well. I don't know whether it was on the 10th of June exactly, as Mr. Milosevic just said. I certainly cannot confirm the authenticity of the entire speech, but the political positions and the principled positions that you referred to were certainly the positions that you upheld and the positions of the SPS, and that is indeed what was considered at the main board; an appeal for dialogue, for cooperation, for a peaceful solution of existing problems. Efforts of the state commission consisting of a commission of the Republic of Serbia headed by Mr. Markovic, that is also not at issue. I was present there, but what actually happened on the ground, I wasn't there, nor can I testify whether this principled policy was actually implemented in the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was -- was it clearly stressed at this meeting and always, at least when the party leadership was involved, that we could be a progressive country, a country developing successfully only if we respect the principle of national equality or ethnic equality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a very short answer to that: Yes. But I must also add that this meeting was held not long after my lengthy tour of Kosovo and the information I conveyed to you as to what was actually happening over there at Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will exhibit the minutes. It can get the next Defence number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the registry to copy this document and return this copy to me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You will have the copy back in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know as to whether ever, throughout all these events, there was any political position to the effect that the Albanians from Kosovo be expelled?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, meetings that I attended of the main board, executive board, meetings with you, I'm not aware of any such position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there ever any plan to expel the Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those are some general questions with which I wish to embark upon the question of Kosovo. I should now like to go on to Bosnia with a few general questions as well. I assume that you followed this so-called trial here, at least partially. I said with regard to Bosnia and Croatia, that we were there concentrating on peace and not war. Is it well known and is it true that Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I personally, invested all our efforts with respect to both Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia to achieve peace as soon as possible? Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the outcome of that was the whole series of peace plans that were offered, either to the Bosnian side, if we're talking about the Serbs in Bosnia, or the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone from Serbia, and when I say "anyone from Serbia," I'm talking from the authorities including the police, the state security, and other bodies, any bodies, did anyone from those bodies instigate, through any activity on its part, the war in Bosnia or Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is rather hard for me to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, when talking about the events in Croatia, did anybody from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or in those days it was still the SFRY, or from Serbia participate in those events in Croatia when those pressures came about on the Serb populations, when people were dismissed, fired from their jobs, when they were eliminated from the constitutions, silent liquidations and everything that was reminiscent of the Ustasha genocide of the Second World War due to which the people were frightened, and with reason. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the Serb population that was in jeopardy at the time, and what they did to protect themselves, did they do so as an act of self-defense?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that they, when I say "they," I mean the Serbs in Croatia, had lived in those areas for centuries?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I'm very familiar with that area, the people who lived there and who are now mostly living in the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true they were not conquering territories on which they did not live or rather that they wanted to defend the territories on which they had lived for centuries?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that apart from the problems we are familiar with, they took up arms to defend themselves, but immediately accepted -- though there were problems of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think these are matters which the Trial Chamber is going to have to decide. I've allowed you to ask the witness's opinion about some of them, but strictly it's irrelevant. Unless he has got direct evidence on matters, he can't give evidence about these things. So if you've got some direct questions, concrete questions to ask, of course, you can, but not evidence of opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Mr. Lilic, with regard to the suffering of the Serbs in Croatia in 1990 and 1991, up to 1995, has many things to say on the basis of his own direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, do you have any direct knowledge as to what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, just briefly, in one sentence, please tell us what was going on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, to put it mildly, when talking about the Serbs in Croatia, not to use too heavy a word, but in view of the percentage of Serbs that lived there, 18 to 22 per cent, today there's less than 2 per cent remaining, so this in itself speaks for itself. On the other hand, I think as early as 1992, thanks to the activities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia, that the Vance Plan was a good opportunity for Krajina, the opportunity was missed in the first place I would say because a part of the leadership of the Republika Srpska Krajina were not serious enough. Of course, that does not justify the two major operations of the Croats and the expulsion of the Serbs from that area through Storm and Flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think you've told us enough in general lines about those matters. What happened to the Serbs in Bosnia as a politician and as a functionary from that time period? You knew that we all referred to Bosnia as Yugoslavia in miniature precisely because it was inhabited by both Serbs, Muslims and Croats. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if we're talking about the time of the SFRY, I think fully reflected the ethnic composition of Serbia until recently. So what you say is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the practice and the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina such as to require a consensus of all three constituent peoples as defined in the constitution regarding all decisions, that is, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the decision on independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was taken without the participation of the Serb people as a constituent people, and that it couldn't be considered lawful and legal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Serbs and Muslims had achieved something that they called a historical agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the details of that agreement, but I do know that it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that all three parties eventually signed - and Carrington was chairing the conference at the time - signed this plan but the plan itself was under the leadership of Ambassador Cutileiro, and all three sides eventually signed it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, and this was not long after the beginning of the war. And I think that, later on, it was the Muslim side that reneged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Cutileiro plan was signed before the beginning of the war, and when the Muslim side changed its mind, recognition occurred, and the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in broad lines, but there were, I think, individual clashes even before the Cutileiro plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that all those initial attacks were mostly such that the victims were Serbs? I'm talking about the incursion into Northern Bosnia, Slavonski Brod, the killing at the wedding ceremony in Sarajevo. The first victims of the war were Serbs, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, yes, and I think that the war in Bosnia actually started with the killing of somebody called Gardovic, if I remember correctly, at a wedding ceremony in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We shall now follow the order in which you testified to the extent that I will be able to keep track of that order, because Mr. Nice did occasionally go from one topic to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're moving to another topic, that would be a convenient time to adjourn. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, in view of the fact that you held one of the highest positions, and afterwards, in fact, the highest position, in those peace efforts, you yourself were also involved in a certain way, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way. I didn't participate in the foreign political diplomatic and in the negotiations themselves, but otherwise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember my letter published in Politika immediately after the outbreak of the war in Bosnia, addressed to the Islamic conference in Istanbul, saying that the Serbs and Muslims were brothers and that the conflict should stop immediately, and that the conflict served only the interests of the enemies of both Serbs and Muslims and that the problems must be resolved by peaceful means?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details, but I do know of that letter, and I do know that its substance was in accordance with what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember my visit to Turkey and the talks I had with the president of Turkey at the time, Ozal, and the Prime Minister Demirel, and my position that Serbia would support every solution that the three peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina agree on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was our political position later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that immediately after that, the international community invested certain efforts and sought our assistance to achieve a peaceful solution, and that as a result of those efforts that lasted several months, I would say, in Athens in the 1st of May, 1993, the Vance-Owen plan was signed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you participated in all the negotiations with representatives of the international community, whichever group we are talking about, then and later, and I do remember that that Vance-Owen plan was initialled in Athens, that it was initialled by Mr. Radovan Karadzic, I believe, in the presence of Mr. Mitsotakis, if I'm not mistaken, and that met with general approval in -- amongst us in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who contributed most to the leadership of the Republika Srpska headed by Karadzic - and the whole delegation of the Republika Srpska was present - who contributed most to them accepting that plan and signing it in Athens?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think certainly you made the greatest contribution, and you have the greatest merit for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that they had the proviso that that signature had to be confirmed by the Assembly of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what you conveyed to us at one of the meetings we had in Belgrade, that there was a possibility for them to betray the trust shown in them by you personally and the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that I went to attend that Assembly meeting in Pale, we drove in the same car, the Greek Prime Minister Mitsotakis and myself, and Mitsotakis invested maximum efforts to help achieve peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that Assembly meeting at Pale should have verified what had been initialled in Athens. And in addition to you yourself and Mr. Mitsotakis, I think that our delegation from the Republic of Serbia included Mr. Dobrica Cosic, Mr. Momir Bulatovic, representing Montenegro, and even I was present, so that I remember that trip very well and our attendance at the Assembly in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were present at that Assembly meeting in Pale.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that I spoke twice at that Assembly meeting in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember all the speakers who took the floor, who were trying to exert pressure, but in inverted commas pressure. I think it was the most reasonable solution which, unfortunately, was not accepted at the time. The effort was to persuade the Assembly majority, if we can talk about the majority, in which the SDS almost held all the seats in the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you're saying is quite correct because with the exception of four members of the Reformist Party, or whatever they were called, the Assembly actually consisted of members who were all SDS members. Do you remember that after my first speech, there was an extensive debate by representatives of the Republika Srpska against the plan, and that I took the floor a second time, insisting that the plan be adopted and explaining why peace was in the interest of all the peoples, including the Serb people, that it was the only option, and that the plan had to be accepted. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I must be even a little more precise, if I may. I think it was quite clear that the Assembly meeting itself had already been prepared so that the plan would not be accepted and that a part of the members acted in that way, and that did require two of your interventions. I think Mr. Dobrica Cosic also spoke, Prime Minister Mitsotakis spoke, Momir Bulatovic, you're taking the floor a second time. In my conviction, almost achieved the result of the plan being accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to ask you because in my second address, I sought to refute the arguments used to reject the plan. And that the Assembly, in spite of its composition and in spite of that atmosphere, responded with applause. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I wanted to say a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then the proposal was put forward by individuals who did not want the plan to be adopted to have a timeout situation. Do you remember that, in order for the SDS deputies' club and its members to be able to consult each other, to confer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a members' club was held. That was the proposal made, although that was superfluous according to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many hours we waited down below for them to hold this members or deputies' club meeting up above, on the storey above? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we even asked, or rather it was -- they asked some of us to attend the club meeting, but that they refused, and they went on conferring for several hours. I can't give you a precise answer. But it was indeed several hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I insisted that we attend this meeting of the deputies' club, and they refused to allow us to take part because the conviction was that we would have our opinions prevail and convince them. Wasn't that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was just slightly different within the context of what you just said in your last sentence. They thought that they wouldn't be able to speak openly and frankly in front of us and that they had already decided not to adopt the plan. So if there were any reservations, it was possible they thought that under our pressure -- not pressure, but by force of argument that the deputies would be prevailed upon to understand that this was the best possible moment and option. And I'm certain from this distance of time that that for the Republic of Serbia was the best way in which to achieve a peace plan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Republika Srpska, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the rigorous sanctions were introduced at the time against us and the Republika Srpska as well and against one and all, in fact, and the war continued in which countless people suffered, many more people lost their lives than had lost them until then, until the conclusion of the Vance Owen plan. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So after this deputy club meeting, the matter was put to vote, and the plan was rejected. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the plan was rejected. This happened in the early hours of the morning, if I remember correctly, or deep into the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After that, in view of the fact that our reactions were highly negative to this kind of wrong decision that had been taken, if I can put it that way, and a tragically erroneous decision, if I might say, we introduced a blockade in order to attempt to force them to reconsider their policy and position and accept the peace plan in the long run. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are confusing the Vance Owen plan and the plan of the contact group, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
