utterances.text: Well, it doesn't really matter, but I'm sure you'll remember that Serbia, and I personally, lent our support to five different peace plans, in fact, which were put forward and placed on the negotiating table, always on the basis of the negotiations that were marathon ones held in Geneva, mostly in Geneva, actually, but in other places too, of course. And that it was not successful.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what is certain when it comes to the Vance Owen plan is that following your decision, we stormed out of the meeting prior to dawn, regardless of the fact that they wanted us to stay on because there was the threat of a Muslim attack, and quite certainly there were a lot of restrictions in 1994 with respect to any assistance from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the war continued, and at the end of the examination-in-chief today, you commented on a note on the records from a meeting of the highest top military leadership and political leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska, as it says. This is the document that you were asked to comment on and that you looked at a moment ago. And the meeting was held on the 22nd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 20. Let the witness have the document first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assumed that he already had the document and that it was in front of him. But of course, he ought to have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, it says that the Yugoslav side was represented at the meeting by: "The president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Zoran Lilic; the Republic of Serbia president, Slobodan Milosevic; the Republic of Montenegro president, Momir Bulatovic; Federal Prime Minister, Dr. Radoje Kontic; Chief of the Army of Yugoslavia General Staff, Momcilo Perisic, General; Federal Minister of Defence, Pavle Bulatovic, and Chief of the FRY President's Military Cabinet, General Slavoljub Susic." And the delegation of Republika Srpska consisted of the following persons: Radovan Karadzic, who was the president; the vice-presidents of Republika Srpska, Nikola Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic; the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik; the Prime Minister, Dusan Kozic; the Foreign Minister, Aleksa Buha; the Commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic; Assistant to the VRS GS Commander for Security, General Lieutenant Zdravko Tolimir; the man in charge for religious affairs, legal information, and moral guidance, Milan Gvero; and for logistics Djordje Djukic, General. And also attending the meeting were the Patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Mr. Pavle, and Irinej Bulovic, the Orthodox bishop; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the meeting well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I asked the representatives of Republika Srpska to inform those of us present as to what had happened at the last meeting of Republika Srpska and the American peace plan was welcomed and the readiness expressed on the part of the delegations of the Republika Srpska together with the delegation of Yugoslavia should take part at the forthcoming international peace conference; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Krajisnik proposed that Koljevic take the floor and expound on the issue. Koljevic considered that on behalf of one and all, this should be done by Radovan Karadzic, president of Republika Srpska. That's what it says here. And then Karadzic goes on to explain that they had a lengthy discussion, there was a lot of fear expressed, not enough confidence, but finally that the conclusions were adopted according to which the Assembly supported the American peace initiative and accepted to -- accepted that people should go to the peace negotiations. They said that they feared that the -- with the delegation becoming part of the Yugoslav delegation, the Muslims would have the advantage. They didn't want to have Republika Srpska lose its legitimacy in the eyes of the international community, that the Serbs could become a national minority. These were all the anxieties that were expressed, and they were all nonsense actually, and I assume you were of that same opinion, were you not? Is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Except for the fact that I think that at that point in time, the Assembly of Republika Srpska had still not reached its decision to go to Dayton, and that was a pretext later on to try and prolong this process and continue negotiations with respect to the delegation's composition, in view of the fact that Karadzic insisted that there were two delegations, one of Republika Srpska, and the other of our own with six members and under pressure from us, that is to say from you, primarily, they accepted and accepted to go to the negotiations as it says in these second minutes or records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Pay attention to a sentence in the middle of that paragraph. On page 2, paragraph 3, it says according to the opinions of Republika Srpska, America wouldn't like the relationships between the Republika Srpska and the FRY of Yugoslavia to improve, it would not suit them. So this sentence, which was just mentioned by the by, in passing here, I hope for you who were well aware of the situation speaks miles. We helped the people, did we not, and we had fairly poor relationships, especially since the Vance-Owen plan, with the leadership of the Republika Srpska; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the party cooperation of the SDS was for the most part with opposition parties in Serbia, that there was never party cooperation between the SPS and the SDS, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, there wasn't party cooperation at the level -- at this level or at any level, but yes, there was party cooperation between the SDS and some opposition parties of the day. I think they are in power in Serbia today, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm so sure you'll remember that Karadzic had criticisms of the media in Yugoslavia and their conduct. He mentioned specifically in the last paragraph - you have that portion - criticisms of the radio which said that the people had finally come to realise what was happening and that they said that the time has come to place matters on healthy foundations, and he emphasises that cooperation between Republika Srpska and Yugoslavia was open and frank and sincere. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and I think that he was promised at the time that the media would change their position somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I should like to draw your attention to page 4 of the same document. They were having a discussion, and the discussion is contained in these minutes, second paragraph. It says, President Slobodan Milosevic referred to speeches made by the previous presenters and assessed that they were still in the slow-thinking phase as regards the direction in which the situation was progressing. We must abide by the key conclusion from the last meeting that now we had to choose between either prompt peace or prompt war. And he added that we only had a few more weeks left and that we were not in a position to discuss principles which we had already debated numerous times with the international community. Should you believe that -- and I'm being quoted here in this record, and it says: "Should you believe that you can reach a solution with Muslims alone, just go ahead and try it. We shall support you, but I doubt that you'll be successful," said President Milosevic, addressing the Republika Srpska leadership. And he once again put forward the conviction that Alija Izetbegovic did not have a strategy for peace, but a strategy for war, and he said that he was working to provoke the Serbs to make some thoughtless move which would make NATO do the work for them. America would like to have peace, it suits them, they would like to have talks, and the model was the five-plus-three makeup, the contact group members representatives of FRY, Croatia, and the Muslims. And I reminded them that proposals were needed to have the Yugoslav delegation include several people from Republika Srpska who would accept peace, who would accept what was discussed and debated at the conference, and the results of the conference itself. And I cautioned to the fact that for the international community, the existence of Republika Srpska was not a prerequisite for the conference but that Republika Srpska ought to be the result of the conference. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was Republika Srpska the result of the conference, in fact? Was that the upshot? It was sanctioned in Dayton?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then I go on to insist that we have a clear-cut stand with respect to the contact group as a plan as the starting point for future negotiations because that was indeed the proposal made by the contact group itself, and I also strove to ensure that there would not be more than two representatives of Republika Srpska, that we should work speedily and expeditiously, and that the peace process had to be continued. And then there is an explanation where Karadzic tells us which the two delegates would be who would take it upon themselves to have the responsibility for such a crucial decision for the entire people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and required that there be six delegates in the delegation of Republika Srpska. We insist once again upon our views, our views and positions were the same, to have a united delegation, including the representatives of Republika Srpska, he said. And then he says at the same time: "The Muslims with the support of NATO will hit us in our positions until our territories are reduced to 20 per cent." And towards the end of that page I once caution and say that there's not much time left, that it is in our interest to reach an agreement because if we fail to do so, there will not be a Republika Srpska either. Because they referred to the constitution, I said there will be neither Republika Srpska, and then I say neither will it have a constitution, to which you refer when you insist upon the fact that you must have the consent of the Assembly on all matters. Then we'll have nothing, we'll end up with nothing. And then of course we get to an explanation. They explain why, why they should just be an appendage to Yugoslavia, and to that I say quite directly, frankly, and to their faces in no meagre terms, I say that is because we have had bad experience with you so far. Isn't that right? Therefore, our insistence was upon what is accepted by the delegation and signed by the delegation must be the final outcome and that we cannot leave any possibility of having a repeat of what happened with the Vance-Owen Plan. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and I think that there was another condition or position put forward that your vote should be the decisive vote if they were to make any reservations on their part, because Karadzic, in part of this conversation, indicates that in the international community there was great concern that the mad Serbs, as he said, from Bosnia could reject this peace plan, too. So I think that this was the purpose of setting the conditions with respect to the composition of the delegation, and that your vote should be the decisive vote, and I think that's what happened at Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, I'd like to draw your attention now to page 8 where Milosevic cautions the leadership of Republika Srpska that his proposals should not be taken to be as his will to impose anything that goes against the grain of the Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he indicated the lack of understanding as to the seriousness of the situation by the leadership of Republika Srpska and did not agree with the views put forward that they had overridden some of their stands of principle in order to go along with Serbia. He said that if they really thought that what they were doing was what they were doing for Serbia and for the SR of Yugoslavia, they were along the wrong road. And vice versa, that everything that the leadership of Yugoslavia was doing should be understood as a service for good, something in the interests and to the advantage of the Serb people as a whole. And Perisic takes the floor - and this is on page 9 - that the fact that people are saying that the international community is conspiring against our own people and that there were situations of excess, that to make the Serbs behave in keeping with the interests of the makers of a new world order, he appealed to reasonable and well-thought-out steps on our part, and then he goes on to advocate the fact that the contact group should not be mentioned specifically but that we ought to enter the peace process as soon as possible. He then cautions that time is running out, that NATO is preparing for its air strikes against Serb positions, and that the land forces would be engaged, that that was not out of the question, and that this was not the right to have discussions and debates among the leadership about details because if the whole world is against us, we must be wise and protect our interests, protect what can be protected. And then President Milosevic suggested to the leadership of Republika Srpska to issue a statement in which two things should be highlighted: Firstly, to criticise the shelling of Sarajevo and the killing of innocent civilians in a stronger manner; secondly, to propose a cessation of hostilities and the withdrawal of heavy artillery to a distance of 20 kilometres from Sarajevo. Do you remember that up until then, in that period of time, officially the government of Serbia on several occasions, and this was made public by the daily press, condemned in the strictest possible terms the bombing of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and not only the government of Serbia, but others, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the government because this is official condemnation. Of course there was condemnation from other quarters as well. And then Karadzic, continuing on from Mladic's elaboration, voiced his opinion that Muslims after the lifting of the Sarajevo blockade will not want to talk and discuss anything with the Serbs. He was opposed to the fact that only Krajisnik and Koljevic be part of the delegation, taking into account that their participation could be manipulated because both were members of the parliament, or rather, the former BiH Presidency under Alija Izetbegovic's power and authority. Milosevic once again warned that if, as of today, the two leaderships did not reach an agreement to go to the peace process, then we ought to know what would await us as a consequence of that. If we don't go to the conference, if we're not there, and if we don't reach an agreement with the opposing side, then the Security Council and NATO would conduct a demarcation arbitrarily as it sees fit. People were upset because, quite obviously the RS leadership did not understand the seriousness facing the Serb people on the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. President Milosevic said: "Your suspicions could cost us dearly. If you don't have any confidence in the best intentions and sincere wishes of the whole Yugoslav leadership, President Lilic, Bulatovic, Kontic and the others who are present here to help you to the best of their ability, then there's no point in discussing this issue any further." Then the patriarch joined in the debate. The patriarch, as a support for the negotiations, and he says it is much more important what is signed than who signs it, although it is good thing for the signatory to be somebody who is trusted and respected by the people. And he reiterated the church's appeal for Serbian unity in the interests of the Serbian people. And then, as there was a lot of pulling and tugging from all sides, I'm sure you'll remember that once I had thanked His Eminence for his wise words, President Milosevic put forward a new proposal that the delegation to represent Serb interests number six members, three from the FRY, and three from Republika Srpska. And to make all this official, he proposed the text of an agreement for these two leaderships, clearly determining the compositions and competence and authority of the delegations involved. Krajisnik was against the formal signing of any mutual agreement between the two leaderships. He said, Why should we have a piece of paper? Is that not a trust of no confidence to the leadership? And President Milosevic told him that he was forced to do so on the basis of experience so far that he had had in agreements with Republika Srpska which did not abide by many oral decisions and agreements and brought us into a difficult situation vis-a-vis the international community. He also said that it would be dangerous to prolong the process, and that time should be bought, but any buying of time worked to the advantage of the enemies. And then he quotes Radovan Karadzic as saying that he always thought he had a better solution. He was prone to waver. And he said that he always thought that if you don't accept the written agreement between the two leaderships, then good luck to you, you can fight alone. I merely wish to draw you to the fact that if you don't accept the proper paper on mutual agreement, President Lilic, myself, Bulatovic, Kontic, Perisic, and the others, we shall only think about the interests of the Republic of Yugoslavia and you do what you want. The responsibility is up to you, history will tell, and you will have to be held accountable to history for your acts. And then Momir Bulatovic goes on to say: "The only way to achieve anything at all is if we have a joint appearance before the world, if we pool our efforts." And Krajisnik ultimately agrees that the joint delegation number six members. And if there is an equal number of votes, there will be no solution. Then I insist upon the fact that as we have a ratio of three to three, it will be the voice of the head of the delegation that will prevail, that is to say, I will have the casting vote. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The president of the FRY, Zoran Lilic, said that such procedure is Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 22710 to 22719. common in the work of delegations, and he quite understands that it is quite understandable that President Milosevic and, as you put it at that time, being the most skillful and most experienced negotiator, decide when and what is to be accepted in the interests of our people. Again, questions concerning a single delegation are raised. A joint delegation with equal decision-making rights, and so on and so forth. The others, the majority, accepted this. The majority of the leadership accepted a single delegation. Then again there was a break at the proposal of Republika Srpska. The atmosphere was tense, and there was uncertainty regarding the final outcome. The discussion was continued in an even more tense atmosphere burdened with apparent suspicion from the RS leadership side that, by accepting the obligation, they would let down the trust of the Assembly's delegates. And in the meantime, I had prepared a text of the agreement that should be signed. And then finally, after I don't know how much time, I don't know how long this went on, again, around 2300 hours, a break was requested. It is obviously angry because of the procrastination and in view of the seriousness of the situation, President Milosevic proposed that the leaders of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia sign the agreement and this way they would confirm that they are working for the general good of the Serb people and all citizens of Yugoslavia without any reservations. The document was signed by the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church, His Holiness Pavle and Bishop Irinej Bulovic. After a long debate in a separate conference room, the leadership of Republika Srpska was joined by the house representatives of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, followed by Patriarch Pavle and Bishop Irinej. They asked that priorities be set forth. Patriarch Pavle also signed the agreement, and we finally reached it. Now I'm asking you not only as a witness and as a participant in this meeting, but as a politician as well who held the top office in the state, was it possible at all -- would it have been possible to have reached Dayton if this step had not been made, this interim step, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one thing is certain, and I have repeated that many times and there is no need for me not to say it today too: There wouldn't have been any Dayton accords if had there not been this much persistence in exerting pressure primarily from your side upon I should perhaps say almost the entire leadership of Republika Srpska because Dr. Koljevic and, I believe, Biljana Plavsic quite soon realised that this should be agreed to. And Karadzic obstinately refused most of the proposals that were made. Two meetings preceded this. Actually, a letter that you got from Karadzic preceded these two meetings, and you could not trust him therefore, in view of everything that had happened until then. And in the letter he accepted that he would make concessions, as he had put it, in terms of withdrawing heavy artillery around Sarajevo, and then at the meeting itself he voiced his reservation, that is to say, that if the artillery is withdrawn, that the Muslims would have an advantage, and so on and so forth. Again, he showed that he was not a person you could trust unless there were such clear-cut positions that are later translated into a specific document stating that there would be a single delegation. The briefest answer would be that Dayton certainly would not have happened had it not been for these meetings. These documents were made at my insistence, and they were composed by General Susic. They were really in great detail and they truly portrayed the atmosphere at these meetings. So everything you have said just now is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear, because at the very beginning of the text, you were nominated as the person who was in the top position, that is, the delegation of the FRY and Republika Srpska, and the FRY delegation is headed by President Zoran Lilic. So it is your responsibility that this should be authentic by all means, and I believe that this is authentic. So your secretary, or rather, the secretary, or rather the head of the military office of the president compiled these minutes, and therefore this is an authentic record.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I highlighted that fact, but my name is the first here, only de jure, and I believe you'll agree to that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will agree. There's no doubt that my efforts in this respect were crucial. I'm not denying it, and it is my understanding that you're not either.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Your efforts, your influence, and as I said, your negotiating abilities in view of all of the negotiations you conducted over all those years in conditions that were not exactly easy. These were important meetings. And certainly, or rather, it is a big question as to whether there would have been any Republika Srpska had it not been for these meetings. Another thing you did not refer to is that the leadership of the Republika Srpska, primarily Mr. Karadzic, did not believe that NATO strikes were possible in the area around Sarajevo. They were cautioned about that too by you in view of the intelligence that you received and that we all had together, that the strikes would follow quite soon after these meetings. And unfortunately, because of their obstinacy, this truly happened only a few hours after this agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After Dayton, you were familiarised with the negotiations that were quite difficult, and that went on for three weeks in quite a bit of detail. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that at that time, I was practically the only person, or rather, the only high-ranking official, if I can use that term, who remained in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The highest ranking official who remained in Belgrade. Well, do you remember that at the first meeting in Dayton, the Muslim delegation proposed that the territory of Republika Srpska be only 37 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the information that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that then the representatives from Republika Srpska invoked the position of the contact group concerning the half/half division, and they were given the following answer: "All questions are open, and there are no obligations that had been taken over from the previous period, that is to say that everything is subject to debate and negotiations." Do you know, then, to what extent an effort had to be made and what kind of negotiations we had to go through in order to reach this half/half solution? I'm asking you this because there is a rather distorted picture that is bandied about among the public, saying that in Dayton, the Serbs got only 49 per cent, and the situation was quite different. And it was quite different. In this 50/50, we then included a significant part of the territories that had already been lost after the NATO strikes and after the collapse that then followed in the army of Republika Srpska. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, several times you started out to say during the examination-in-chief something in relation to Srebrenica but Mr. Nice interrupted you. Now I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not fair. He didn't. The witness was allowed to give his views, although of course they are only views. He's only giving an opinion about it. What Mr. Nice rightly pointed out was that it's only a matter of opinion, it will be for the Trial Chamber to determine the matter. But yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I believe that that is not a correct interpretation because this is not the opinion of Mr. Lilic; this is a question of what he knows in relation to the high office he held. He is not the usual kind of witness that Mr. Nice brings here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You can ask the witness questions, of course, about his knowledge, his detailed knowledge of the matters. But certainly he was giving an opinion yesterday. But you ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to answer my question. What was it that you knew with regard to that? What did the leadership of Serbia know? What did the leadership of Yugoslavia know? Because what happened was truly dramatic, tragic. So I'm not asking you for your opinion only because, as you can see, opinions are not allowed. I'm just asking you about your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presented what I knew yesterday and today. And I also established that no one from the leadership of Serbia and Yugoslavia could have issued such an order, and we were not aware of this either. I also presented my own impressions regarding this tragic event several days later at a meeting I had with you. I said that you were more than angry, shaken, and you used the following sentence, or rather to this effect: "These crazy Serbs from Pale" - and you were primarily referring to the leadership of Republika Srpska or part of the leadership - "I cannot believe that they did something like this." I also presented my impression that I do not believe that in any capacity you took part in any such thing. And quite simply, no one on our side was informed about that unless there was some private communication along certain lines between certain individuals who were outside our day-to-day meetings in a way. I don't know what expression to use really in this context. I think I explained this already: The Srebrenica case is a truly tragic case. It was done by individuals. That is my opinion, that is my impression, and it is certain that this Chamber will make a final ruling on that. There was no organised participation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, at least not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the leadership of Republika Srpska, when we asked what happened and how it was possible that something like that happened, they answered that they were not aware of this either?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. I tried to say it today, and I said it during my examination yesterday, so my answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to go back to the beginning of your examination in chief from yesterday, then. Mr. Nice asked you about the role that was played by the Socialist Party of Serbia in the legislative process. And he asked whether it had a leading role. Is it being contested that a party that has parliamentary majority in any parliamentary democracy does, of course, have a leading role in legislation, or rather the work of parliament?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the answer I gave, and that's the explanation I gave. That is the essence of parliamentary life in Serbia, that the parliamentary majority which was almost absolute during the first term, as far as the Socialist Party of Serbia is concerned, I think we had a total of 194 seats, if I'm not mistaken, and we passed legitimate decisions in the Assembly, and we certainly influenced the bringing of laws. And after all, this was our right therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you president of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the Republika Srpska, that's what I became in January of 1993, after the elections, the extraordinary elections that were held in 1992 that you agreed to, although they were not regular elections, but you did this in response to demands put forth by the opposition. And at that time, the Republican Assembly, I think, had over 100 seats, or rather the SPS had over 100 seats. And then we had a coalition within parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, we established a minority government. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we had a minority government. And in parliament, we were seeking ways and means of getting the necessary 126 votes, which was only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Later on, the Serb Radical Party brought about a crisis in the National Assembly, and then at the proposal of the government, I dissolved the Assembly and new elections were held.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when we were -- when you were president of the Assembly, we did not have a majority in the Assembly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, we did not have a parliamentary majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that sense, consultations and preparations in bodies of the National Assembly were held in parliamentary committees at the proposal of the government with our participation which could not have been absolute, only relative. We were relatively the biggest party, but we did not have the possibility of reaching decisions on our own in relation to bills and laws. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. During that term in the Assembly of Serbia, our participation was not dominant. We did not have a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then, after the extraordinary elections were held, we were -- we had almost reached half of the seats in parliament, and then we had a coalition with the New Democracy Party.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I'm not mistaken, we had 123 seats then. It is true that we did have a coalition with the Nova Demokratija of Dusko Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and his party had a total of seven seats?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we got the necessary majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The necessary majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The necessary absolute majority in parliament. Now, well, I don't know why Mr. Nice highlighted this as something really important in your statement, but you say towards the end of 1995, the Yugoslav Left was established. And the Yugoslav Left entered a coalition with us before the 1996 elections. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But if you allow me to explain, the 123 seats from the previous Assembly, if I can. It is certain that it is indispensable to have an absolute majority of 126 MPs in order to fully control the work of parliament from the point of view of the political party that has this majority. However, in view of the rule that for the most part, decisions are passed by a majority vote of the MPs present, then this majority didn't have to guarantee a particular outcome. I wanted to explain this so that there would not be any wrong ideas in respect of what I said previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Yugoslav Left was established at that time in 1995 by 23 parties that had a left orientation, workers' parties, socialist, social democratic, and so on and so forth? It wasn't the way you put it, that this was done by me or my wife.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that it was formed by 23 parties. I do know what influence it wielded in the political and economic life of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I do know that they never took part independently at elections before 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, and because it's not correct, I'll remind you now. My impression is not that you're saying something incorrect intentionally, but only because, probably under the influence of the present-day propaganda, you forget the facts as they were. But I'm quite sure that when I remind you, you will remember. So please, don't think that I consider anything you say as malicious.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know very well I was never malicious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you as I have the programme here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you have any interest, I have it in English also, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says, on the 23rd of July, it was founded out of 23 left-oriented parties and a large number of individuals who joined the movement on an individual basis. This left was seen flexibly: Communist, socialist, social democrat, the wide spectrum, right up to the greens. And then it says: "The Yugoslav Left is not an expression of something new, only in terms of organisation. It is also new in the understanding of its theoretical basis. By its theoretical basis, the Yugoslav Left considers every idea of freedom or every thought contributing to the liberation of man, of violence, poverty, exploitation, humiliation, ignorance, contained in philosophy, science, religion, and art." Do you remember that, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, but I have no reason not to believe that that is what it says in their programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll let you have a look at it as I do believe that this was the best programme drafted by the left in Europe at the end of the last century. They say at the very beginning, "It is possible for humanity to enter the third millennium respecting and using everything liberating and progressive, that it has -- man has achieved by thought and work in the course of his development regardless of what part of the world he may be in, and what time he may have achieved it, that is regardless of which social system the liberating and progressive was created in. In that respect, we attach the greatest importance to the idea of material prosperity, which is the supreme idea of a capitalist society, a civil civilisation on the one hand, and the idea of equality as a supreme value of socialist theory and practice on the other. "United, these two ideas could change the world and take man forward into a new peaceful and prosperous society." Therefore, the programme is quite extensive and lengthy. I can't quote all of it, but this obviously is not in harmony with the intrigues that are being bandied about and that are part of the struggle against the left in the world in general. Now, let us back come to what you're saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we do, you've produced this programme. Let the witness just see it just to confirm it is what it says it is, and we'll exhibit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give it to you in English, Mr. May, for you, and to the witness, I'll give him a Serbian copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have it both. Let the witness see the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quite sure that the witness doesn't doubt that I quoted the text correctly. But, of course, he can look at it. He can see for himself what I have quoted. I have marked the passages at the beginning. I don't believe that he doubts my correctness, correctness of my quotations. Anyway, it is a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could we have the next number, please. Wait a minute. Let's just have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 143, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lilic, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Thank you, Mr. May. I do not doubt at all the correctness of the programme that Mr. Milosevic spoke about, nor the principles of the left. I do not wish what I'm going to say to be seen as a political speech. I'm a leftist by orientation, and those principles have very close to my heart, and I have been and I remain a leftist regardless of the fact that I am no longer in the establishment. I didn't speak about the programme of the Yugoslav Left, the correctness of options and ideology and -- that is contained in the programme. What I spoke about is the influence of individual people from the Yugoslav Left on the SPS and the state as a whole. And I could say quite freely, regardless of whether we will agree on that or not, I will refer to the abuse that was made by many people from the Yugoslav Left of their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We will come to that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I wasn't talking about the programme of the Yugoslav left, and I wasn't talking about the correctness of that programme otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But since you mentioned my wife, and my wife was exclusively involved with writing, and she wrote this programme, and that is her role in the Yugoslav Left. She was not responsible for the organisation or the financing or any - I don't know how to put it - material activities. But mental activities that she was committed to as an intellectual, and she is the author of this programme of the Yugoslav Left. Now, as you have said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. Can you help us as to that, Mr. Lilic? Is that right? Do you know, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether Mrs. Markovic wrote the programme. I assume she did, and I don't think that is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you've said that the Yugoslav Left did not take part in the elections independently until 2000, I just wish to remind you that the Yugoslav Left was in a coalition at the elections in 1996, a coalition that was officially called the Socialist Party of Serbia, the Yugoslav Left, the New Democracy, Slobodan Milosevic. That was the official title; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that that included SPS, JUL, the New Democracy under my name, all three were together, this coalition, you said that in view of that, there was no basis on which to judge the share of the Yugoslav Left in that coalition, the contribution of the Yugoslav Left within that coalition. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I believe that somebody -- if somebody forms a coalition and takes part in the elections as a coalition, it is difficult to assess the constituent behind the component parts of the coalition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is quite correct, and in principle, that is quite in order. I just wish to remind you that precisely for that reason, because it was difficult to assess the support and the share in the powers, except on the basis of the criteria of the quality of the cadres elected, and the same principle applied to all, a yardstick of participation in the authorities was also the fact that JUL took part independently at local elections in 1996, except in Belgrade, and these were held simultaneously with the general elections, so it participated in the local elections, and at those local elections, their candidates for municipal MPs won more than 400.000 votes. So this was a concrete criterion on the basis of which it was possible to evaluate the contribution they had in the elections in which they took part as part of a coalition. They had more than 800 municipal deputies in various municipalities in Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Okay, stop. The witness can't possibly assimilate all this if you go on so long. Would you come to a concrete question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, I will. I think that, Mr. May, you underestimate the witness and his knowledge. He's very familiar with all these things. He held the highest political positions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt, but we aren't. We can't follow it either. So let's get to a concrete point and put it shortly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can I remind you, therefore, that when simultaneously with the elections you referred to there were local elections and this party won a total of 400.000 votes, no, over 400.000 votes? Do you remember that now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of those figures that were used and referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you said yesterday that representatives of the Yugoslav Left who were coalition partners in the coalition SPS JUL New Democracy held key positions, I asked my associate to get for me from Belgrade the composition of the government at the federal and republican level, and we have that here, for several dates because certain reconstructions had to be made. And they have been faxed, but since the composition of governments in published in the Official Gazette, they are elected by the Assembly, so all this can be checked out in the Official Gazette. For instance, the government of the Republic of Serbia in August 1997, you will remember that, and I will let you have a look at the list. I just crossed out one name here because it was repeated twice under 30 and under 34. The same name is given twice. So I assume the typists made an error. But anyway, Mirko Marijanovic, the Prime Minister, who is a member of the SPS, wasn't he, then? Then, Dragomir Tomic, Minister Coordinator, also SPS; Slobodan Radulovic, vice-premier of New Democracy; Professor Doctor Ratko Markovic, vice-president, SPS; Svetozar Krstic, vice-president from New Democracy; Milutin Stojkovic, vice-president from the SPS; Vlajko Stojiljkovic, vice-president and Minister of the Interior, also SPS; Borislav Milacic, Minister of Finance, SPS; Arandzel Markicevic, Minister of Justice, JUL. I don't need to read out all the names, but the whole government consists of 38 names, actually 37, because Ivan Sedlak is a minister without portfolio from JUL, but he is not a Serb. He's from JUL. He's a member of JUL. That is the Yugoslav Left. I will give you this list to look at. So in this whole cabinet, there were one, two, three, four, five, six JUL members of which two are without portfolio. So out of 37, 6 of them. So that is less than 20 per cent. As for the ministers from JUL, one is Vladimir Ljubicic, who is Minister of Tourism; Arandzel Markicevic, Minister of Justice; Bratislava Morina, Minister for Family Welfare; Ljeposava Milicevic, Minister of Health; Zoran Modric, Minister for Local Self-government; and there is Ivan Sedlak and Andrija Milisavljevic, ministers without portfolio. And there are two nonparty ministers, Professor Radmila Milantijevic, for information, Milan Bego, Minister for Economic Relations and Property Transformation, also a nonparty member. So not a single key department is held by the left, the Yugoslav Left. And the numbers I have given are as they are on this list. Now, let us look at the federal government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we won't. Let the witness see the list which you have been reading out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume this will refresh your memory. I myself couldn't remember offhand, but I know that it wasn't as you put it, and that is why I asked for this list.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume the list is correct. There is no reason for me to doubt it. The only thing is whether I was talking about the composition of the government or key positions throughout the territory of Serbia. I think it was the latter. If I just may finish, I also said that individual members of the SPS were the people who implemented the Yugoslav Left's policy within the SPS, and one of those is certainly Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic who was formerly a member of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was one of the founding members.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of the people who were later in JUL were in the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you had excellent relations with the Yugoslav Left?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not. If that had been so, I wouldn't have lived through everything I did after 1996. I didn't wish to enter this polemics between JUL and the SPS. I thought that you would agree that the SPS was the dominant political party, that all the mandates belong to the suspects, that JUL never participated in the elections independently except in 2000, that it won .38 per cent of the votes. And I still claim that it held key positions in the government of Republic of Serbia, and the federal government, and in other institutions, but that is not in dispute. What is in dispute is whether they abused those positions or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you challenge any of the facts written here, including this, that they had more than 400.000 votes in 1996 at the local elections? Do you challenge that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been through that. Let's -- we'll produce this document now. Which government is this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment, wait a moment. We'll have it exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 144, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now have a look at the federal government, numbering 21 members. It has only two members who belonged to JUL in the federal government in August 1997. And they were Vukovic and Markovic, who before joining JUL was in the Ministry for Foreign Affairs in charge of economic relations. Nebosja Markovic was a prominent businessman. So 2 out of 21. You can look at that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The rest were SPS and DPS from Montenegro, and the Prime Minister was Rade Kontic who was from Montenegro. We have to hurry up.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment, Mr. May, regarding this government is similar to the comment I made regarding the previous government. Here, too, there are SPS members who were absolutely in the function of the Yugoslav Left which need not mean anything, but let me say something about Mr. Vukovic. Through him, all foreign trade arrangements at the level of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia went through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he was Minister for Foreign Trade, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness finish, and we'll deal with this in an orderly way. Yes, Mr. Lilic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was speaking of the significance of the positions held by the members of the leadership of the Yugoslav left. At that point, that was one of the most important positions in the federal government. The quantity is not important, it's the quality of the positions, and that is a fact, without entering into the programme orientation of the Yugoslav Left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We won't dwell on that any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're leaving that document, we'll exhibit it, and then we'll adjourn, because the time has come for an adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 145, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic, I think we agreed a moment ago that without a doubt, the Socialist Party of Serbia was the leading political force in Serbia throughout the material time. And I would also go as far as to say that it was the largest party in the Balkans. Do you share that view and assessment of mine, that the Socialist Party of Serbia in all those difficult times performed its role honourably, and in the best interests of the people and all citizens of and inhabitants of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree that the Socialist Party of Serbia really did give an enormous contribution to the stabilisation of overall events and the situation not only in the territory of the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia but further a field as well, that it was the most important party, and that it was precisely for that reason that I said that according to its merits, it didn't actually get as much rights in the elections as befitted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever happen to hear, and I'm not talking about the top leadership of the Socialist Party of Serbia alone, but of any other leadership of the Socialist Party of Serbia having assumed positions and attitudes which were contrary to its programme, the interests of the citizens and people, or contrary to the interests of any ethnic community at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any case like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to remember that in the membership of the Socialist Party of Serbia at that time, too, and as far as I know, that's the case today as well, that there were many members from other national communities, ethnic communities, both Hungarians and Croats, and Albanians, and Turks, and Goranis, and Romanis, Romanians, Ruthenians, and so on, Muslims, et cetera? And in Serbia, there are a large numbers of ethnic communities living there, and there was not a single ethnic community which did not have its representative in the Socialist Party of Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did speak about that, and I tried to explain how strong the Socialist Party of Serbia was, and the fact that it had almost 10.000 local committees, boards. And as far as its membership, it was truly a heterogenous party and within the frameworks of that party, you would find members of all the ethnic groups, both majority ethnic communities and minority ethnic communities living on the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that not mean, then, that the Socialist Party of Serbia in that way expressed the profoundest interests of all the citizens of Serbia, both by virtue of its structure and by virtue of its composition, judging by its programme, and the things it actually did in practice?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday during the examination-in-chief something that I have heard for the first time, I must say, and I saw that figuring in your statement as well. What you mention is this: You used the term "shadow government," I believe. As far as I know, shadow governments are set up by opposition parties. Why would a government in power set up a shadow government? So what kind of shadow government are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that context, Mr. Milosevic. I think that I understood it well. I used the term figuratively, which is used in the vernacular during our conversations that the people who had privileges, the privilege of having frequent consultations with you were, to all intents and purposes, a form, a part of that government. Not in the official sense of a shadow government, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was no secret that I had a so-called coordination meeting at least once a week. I assume you'll remember that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you could see from the statement that was handed to you that I said it sometimes took place once a week and sometimes more frequently, as the situation required.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes once a week, sometimes less, sometimes more, that's not essential. But you give the names of people who took part in these meetings, probably not all their names, but you did enumerate them correctly. You said Mirko Marijanovic, he was one, he was the Prime Minister, in fact, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you mentioned Dragan Tomic, the president of the National Assembly. Right? Then, there's Milomir Minic, and I jotted this down in the order you gave those names. And Milomir Minic, I jotted down his rank as being president of the federal parliament, or rather, the lower house of the federal parliament, the chamber of citizens. Then there's Milan Milutinovic, president of the Republika Srpska; Zivadin Jovanovic, Foreign Minister. Gorica Gajevic, the Secretary-General of the Socialist Party. Nikola Sainovic, the vice premier of the federal government, who was from Serbia. So those then were the top officials of the Socialist Party at the same time, and the top state officials who attended these coordination meetings in view of the fact that they were at the head of important institutions themselves independently, so this was a chance to exchange information and opinions and to consult one another. So is there anything that would be out of the ordinary in that -- in that practice or something that was unusual for any country?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that I said that anything was unusual or out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you for the answer. Let's move on now, then, please. I think you said quite correctly, explained quite correctly a thesis that is heard and underlined very often here. You know that people like to put forward a position here that is ascribed to the Serbs by ascribing blame to the Serbs for the alleged intention of setting up some sort of a Serb state with only the Serbs, and the slogan of "All Serbs in one state" is usually bandied about in that context. Is it true and correct that the fact that when we say all Serbs to live in one state, this referred to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in fact, and therefore it was our policy at the times that you're testifying about, from 1990 to the year 2000, and in 1990 when the crisis in Yugoslavia started, it related to Yugoslavia, that there was an additional interest on the part of Serbia to safeguard and retain Yugoslavia because it was a country in which all Serbs lived together in one state?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I talked about yesterday when I said that it was precisely that Yugoslavia, that is to say, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which allowed all the Serbs to really live in a single state, in one country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to any of the leaderships, did anybody anywhere ever launch any kind of idea about a Greater Serbia of some kind? Did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not the political positions of the Socialist Party of Serbia, and none of us personally, as far as I know, put that forward. They were the positions of some other political parties, however, or some other leaders outside the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said not ours meaning not the SPS's positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we have been provided with an enormous number of documents here, I'm going to skim over some of them because I have to do so. But could you tell me this, please, give me an answer to a very general question to begin with: In any of the documents that you have been given access to that have been presented to you here, including the documents that you just identified as recognising, is there any mention of any decision which was reached unlawfully or illegally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just commented on one document for which I said that I didn't recognise it and that I was surprised from the aspects of what you're saying now if the document is correct, so I don't know. The document refers to some kind of monies issued from the National Bank of Yugoslavia, large amounts of money, but it wasn't a document either from the Republika Srpska or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The second document that we looked at was a document in which Perisic, General Perisic is writing a letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Perisic's letter. I don't mean that. We'll come to that in due course later on, and we'll see how far there are grounds for that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't know the number of documents that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to all the documents presented here. Is there anything unlawful in them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I was able to see, if we're talking about the same documents, and I assume we are, then no, there is nothing unlawful or illegal in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the following: You said in view of the fact that these were exact facts, the constitution of Serbia was adopted before that of Yugoslavia and of Montenegro, too, and they were not formally dovetailed and harmonised, that is true. However, do you happen to remember that in the constitution of Serbia, as far as I know, and you'll perhaps remember this better than me, it is Article 136, I believe, which stipulates as follows: That Serbia within the composition of Yugoslavia, that the authorisations provided for by the constitution -- under the constitution of Yugoslavia are to be implemented at the level of Yugoslavia regardless of whether they were provided for by the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, because it implied all the authorities and competencies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that article. I don't think it was Article 136. 136 does indeed describe the authorisations, I think, of the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia, but I'm sure that kind of article exists, the contents of what you say, but I'm not sure it was Article 136, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The witness testifying before you here indicated that according to some sort of law, I had the right to give out decorations of some kind as president of the Republic of Serbia. Now, as I never in my capacity as president of the Republic of Serbia gave any decorations to anybody, do you ever remember me giving out decorations when I was president of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember you gave out decorations even to the people you promised them, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that goes for me as president of Serbia, too, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it implies both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the president of the Republic had the right to promote generals and officers first-class, which is not being challenged at all. The promotion of officers first-class is a ceremonial act, and it refers to all those who have completed military academy and joining the army with the lowest officer's rank, and they are being taken in as officers of Yugoslavia once they complete their military academies. A whole new generation of officers in the JNA, and this is an official ceremony and decree signed by the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this generation who has graduated, every new generation graduating from the military academy, this final ceremony is defined by the president and signed -- this decree signed to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were also asked something in connection with the period when Dobrica Cosic was president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and you were asked about the existence of a state council which he had set up. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That particular body did not -- was not founded pursuant to the Yugoslav constitution. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it was the principal reason for which you did not when you yourself became president of Yugoslavia continue to utilise that body or to appoint or nominate it again. There was no reason to do so. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I adhered to the constitutional provisions regarding the authority of the president, and as far as I was concerned I didn't see the need for the existence of that particular council. That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were then asked by Mr. Nice during your term of office how many times the Supreme Defence Council met. Your answer was over 50. He said 53. You said over 50. There's no need to quibble over the number of meetings. I'm sure that that many were indeed held, roughly. But at all those meetings, various issues were discussed, various subjects placed on the agenda as proposed by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and so on. Now, was there a single -- there were many generals there who were promoted, many of them were relieved of their duties, too. Now, throughout that whole time, all the time that you were president of the FRY and Supreme Defence Council, was there a single instance in which a general was promoted or relieved of duty at my own insistence personally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all promoted along with agreement from the members, all the members of the SDC, the Supreme Defence Council. And the agenda of the SDC was composed very often from the presidents of the republics who were members of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They didn't all only come from the general staff and president of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I ever place an item on the agenda of the SDC at all, myself personally?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the agenda for the SDC was dovetailed usually amongst all of us together. I would propose it, you would accept it or something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was standard procedure, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, let me just say that the Supreme Defence Council is quite a specific body, and it's difficult to speak about minutes or records of those meetings because I don't have agreement to comment them. But they had specific relationships, and they focussed on an acceptance of the contact group for Republika Srpska, for example, and I think that particular meeting was held at your proposal, and you wanted all the members of the team to be present, the chief of staff, the army commanders, the senior staff, and of course you, Momir Bulatovic, and Mr. Kontic was there, too, so that was quite a specific meeting, and that is why it comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But that was exclusively as a function of achieving a peaceful solution, was it not, for Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was geared to inform all the members of the Yugoslav army about the behaviour and conduct of the leadership at Pale, and yes it was with the aim of having a peaceful solution and accepting the contact group plan. I think we're talking about 1994 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that it was in order for the leadership, the members, the top military staff, to become informed with our peace efforts and endeavours and for them to understand the policy being waged with respect to reaching a peaceful solution generally? And we had problems on that score in Bosnia and the leadership at Pale?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that we can add anything negative to that. I think the meeting was highly necessary, just like many others that were geared towards establishing peace in the area as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice asked you, and I wrote this down because we are talking about these meetings of the Supreme Defence Council now: "How did the accused impose his own will on the Supreme Defence Council, the way in which he did that? How did the accused influence the Supreme Defence Council?" Now, tell me, did I impose any will of my own on the Supreme Defence Council? Did I do anything outside the framework of the rights that I had as a member of the Supreme Defence Council to take part in its work and to present my opinions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not do anything outside the rights that you had as a member of the SDC, except that that right of membership was dominant. I don't think that at any point in time, or from any point of view should your dominant role be denied -- your dominant role be denied. And Serbia's influence over everything that was going on in Yugoslavia was more dominant than that of Montenegro, although you always try to find ways and means of sorting things out with Bulatovic. So the position you held, the office that you held was dominant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm certainly not denying that I had a dominant position which was derived from some kind of authority that I had acquired, I assume. However, the question was whether I imposed some will of my own to you? When one uses this term, "to impose one's will upon someone," it means that the other party does not agree to that but is compelled to agree to something.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you compelled to accept something because I was advocating it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing was forced upon anything at the Supreme Defence Council. I repeated this several times, all decisions that were reached were reached by consensus, at least while I was president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. As for your authority, I referred to it a short while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not denying it. I'm not denying it at present either. You explained that the relations between Bulatovic and Djukanovic were disrupted, and that that in a way affected the functioning of the federation because later on there was a split within the party as well, the part that remained along with Bulatovic remained in the federal government, and this was also apart from the leadership in the Republic of Montenegro. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, Djukanovic did come to meetings of the Supreme Defence Council, and he did carry out his duties. Sometimes, he didn't, of course, but for the most part, he would come. Is that well known?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he attended a few meetings in the beginning, and that later on, he did not come. It's just the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to draw your attention to the following, because Mr. Nice talked about it, and you commented upon it. These are the records of the 6th of session of the Supreme Defence Council. It's a very long record. I'm not going to comment upon all its points. It's minutes from the 6th session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 4th of October, 1998, present Slobodan Milosevic, Milan Milutinovic, Milo Djukanovic, however let's be quite specific about this. Let everyone see this clearly. The only members of the Supreme Defence Council are the three presidents. Isn't that right? Everybody else is simply present at the meeting of Supreme Defence Council sessions, and they cannot reach any decisions at the Supreme Defence Council. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I should correct this a bit. The only members of the Supreme Defence Council with the right to vote are the three presidents. But there's really no purpose unless the chief of general staff is there and the Minister of Defence, at least. If we were even to exclude the Federal Foreign Minister, and I think that later on as the new rules of procedure were being adopted, that is how you treated their presence as well. For professional reasons, primarily. As for decision making --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Practice was translated into a new set of rules and procedure. Does that -- did that mean that there would be a sharing of responsibility then? How can you talk about sharing of responsibility, the constitution clearly stipulates whose responsibility is what. If the practice that had already existed was translated into new rules of procedure, that has nothing to do with sharing responsibility.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council that I chaired and whose member you were as well, precisely functioned the way you defined it later in the rules of procedure on the 23rd of March, 1999, so it was exactly in accordance with those principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I hope that you have these minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is the 4th of October, 1998, in the Serb version, it is the page that is marked by a number ending in 459. "The president of the FRY, Slobodan Milosevic, presented our general orientation yet again that all pending issues should be resolved by peaceful means and he presented some of the main arguments supporting this orientation. First of all, the cessation of armed operations."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 7 of 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's make sure we have all got the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's page 7 of 10, right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Make sure the witness has it, too. Mr. Lilic, do you have the passage? Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, "he presented the general orientation that all pending issues should be resolved by peaceful means, and he presented some of the main arguments supporting such an option. First, the end of all armed operations." Let me just briefly comment upon this. In The beginning of October, practically this so-called KLA, or rather this terrorist organisation had been defeated. And armed operations had ceased. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the kind of information that was coming in from the people who were in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So first of all, the cessation of armed operations. "Secondly, withdrawal of forces to locations of permanent bases according to the cessation of terrorist actions which is part of our agreement with Russian President Jeljcin. Third, openness of the entire area to free movement of UNHCR members and members of the International Red Cross in order to make it possible to assist in resolving humanitarian issues. Fourth, our readiness for dialogue and resolving problems by peaceful means. All four requests from -- were met from our side despite our criticism in view of this resolution because we do not constitute a threat to peace for neighbouring countries or do we jeopardise their safety. That is what was contained in the resolution. Do you share this view, that we did not constitute any threat to peace for neighbouring countries or that we jeopardised their safety and security?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely; we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we met all four requests, although we did have certain criticism vis-a-vis the resolution precisely because we did not constitute a threat to peace in neighbouring countries, and I say they're not even angry when we stated the accusations for this are unfounded because they had underestimated Albanian terrorism in Kosovo. And then it says, Milosevic reminded that the operations ceased last Monday, that is to say six days ago, anti-terrorist units were returned to barracks, full freedom of movement was ensured not only for UNHCR and activists of the International Red Cross but also for diplomatic missions, even for the representatives of the media, which was not even one of the things called for by the resolution. Now, only the obligations -- this is really important: Only the obligations of Albanian parties and movements were not fulfilled, namely, items 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6.
