Item 7 refers to Albania, but it still tries to bring in military equipment and ammunition into our country, and our border units are efficiently preventing this. So we have fulfilled everything that the resolution called for on our part. All of this was confirmed in the letter of our Minister of the Interior to the UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who will submit a report to the Security Council. And then it says that I reminded the persons attending this meeting of the meeting I had with the ambassadors of the contact group member countries, and I affirm the standpoints of the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia about the resolution of the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija, I also informed the members of the Supreme Council with Russia's positions, whose delegation I had received that day. The Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ivan Ivanov, was there on the delegation, and also the Defence Minister, Igor Sergejev, they presented Russia's standpoint that they would veto a Security Council resolution if one were to be proposed in connection with air strikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They expect us to affirm what we have done by now in the implementation of Resolution 1199 and our readiness for dialogue. Then I say that at the forthcoming session of both chambers of the Federal Assembly, a consensus has to be reached regarding strategic decisions relating to Kosovo and Metohija. We expect that the Yugoslav Assembly will adopt conclusions that will affirm our decisiveness, et cetera. So the Federal Assembly is expected to react in this way as opposed to what is being alleged here. It was not excluded from all of this. So the session is attended by Milutinovic and Djukanovic, both. This is a session held in October 1998. And the conclusion, I'm referring to the page that ends in 61: "Yugoslavia is firmly committed to peace and it is prepared to resolve by peaceful means all pending issues, but if we are attacked we are going to defend the country by all means." That was adopted as the conclusion of this meeting unanimously. And two paragraphs down, it says that both members of the Supreme Defence Council, the president of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic, and the president of Montenegro, Mile Djukanovic, accepted this proposal made by President Milosevic. So this is a decision of the Supreme Defence Council which pertains to the defence of the country. If the country is attacked, then a decision was passed unanimously in terms of what would be done then. Mr. Lilic, is there anything controversial here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the presentation, the minutes, the subject, the conclusion is concerned, I believe that there is nothing controversial. However, as far as we are concerned, we in Serbia, we probably misassessed Russia's position, that they would veto a resolution by the Security Council and also that the campaign would last shorter than we thought, that it did last longer than we thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that was not a decision that we adopted, that was not our conclusion. On the contrary, we said that if we are attacked, we are going to defend the country, but before that, our main position is that we are going to try to resolve things by peaceful means, and we also met the four requirements as I had presented them. Now, I would like to clarify that part of your testimony that has to do with assistance to the army of Republika Srpska and the Serb army of Krajina and the 30th and 40th personnel centres respectively. Since there are quite a few insinuations here in this connection, is it correct that in terms of our engagement, if it were to be defined in a single word, it is only the word "assistance" that can be used? Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that practically all armies created in the territory of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - the Croatian army, the Muslim army, and the Slovenian army, and the Macedonian army, and of course the army of Yugoslavia - were created basically from the former JNA, at least as far as the officer personnel is concerned, and everything that the JNA consisted of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be put that way in relation to the JNA, but I think that all republics also had their Territorial Defences, and then the armies of the republics grew out of that. And as for the officers's corps, yes, of course it came from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this materiel assistance through which we expressed our solidarity with the former members of the JNA who had stayed behind and defended their republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Krajina was only reduced to this welfare aspect, if I can put it that way; the rights they acquired in terms of their salary, their social insurance, and the livelihood of their families depended on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that in detail yesterday, and you have practically confirmed in a way most of what I had said. And that is the point why the 30th and 40th personnel centres were established. But also to bear in mind the resources that were being allocated for the families that were in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Perhaps I still owe a small explanation in addition to that. When the word "centre" is used, it's not a sophisticated facility that is used for training or for putting up a large number of people. It was simply military code VP 3001, and the 40th centre was military post code 4001, and this was also in Belgrade. So this is a brief additional explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Because I even did not know that all of this was just an office and the other one in another office. But it is quite clear that this only meant keeping records of the materiel assistance that was given in relation to the rights acquired until then in the JNA that had existed until then in terms of their salaries and their social insurance. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The fact is that this centre was established after -- after the contact plan was adopted in 1994, rather, when it was not adopted in 1994 and when we ceased to operate as we did until then. And I think that the centres continued to function until the 28th of March, 2001, when President Kostunica abolished this altogether as this annex was being prepared in terms of the cooperation between the army of Yugoslavia and the army of Republika Srpska, and it was supposed to be based on an agreement on special ties between the army of Yugoslavia and the army of Republika Srpska, and this was signed, if I'm not mistaken, the end of February or the beginning of March 1997. And this council of cooperation was established then, and I think that you were elected president of that council, so that is to say that the centre continued to exist until 2001. And the annex was prepared like the annex that had already been worked out between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you just confirm this with a yes or no, this was in accordance with the Dayton accords, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I omitted to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign that agreement with the representative of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed that agreement with Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik in a ceremonial hall in the Presidency of Serbia. I remember it well because I attended that ceremony. It was an agreement on relations between FRY and Republika Srpska based on the Dayton accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to this aid that we were extending as a key matter arises here which needs to be answered and you are quite competent to provide that question. Did the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in any way have a command role in relation to the staff of the Army of Republika Srpska or over the main staff of the Serbian Army of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is simply impossible. If all our normative and legal decisions were abided by, the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia could not be placed in such a decision, and by decision of the Supreme Defence Council that matter was never raised or discussed, so my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because various tables were drawn here and various patterns and diagrams in which the general staff of the Army of Yugoslavia appears at the top, then below it, the main staff the VRS, et cetera, because the intention is to give the impression that these were united armed forces commanded from Belgrade. Will you please comment on that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to see any such diagrams, but such a statement simply does not correspond to the truth or the factual situation, and it was quite impossible without the knowledge of the Supreme Defence Council and an appropriate decision by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've cleared that up. Mr. Nice asked you what kind of control I had, I, Slobodan Milosevic, over the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, et cetera. You answered that the word control could not be used. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you answered that you had some influence, but it was insufficient for them to accept the peace plans. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that my contacts and endeavours were directed, to the extent I was able, and I used my influence sometimes greater, sometimes lesser, but it was always directed towards seeking a peaceful solution and the acceptance of peace plans. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there's no question that you had influence, and that I was present in situations that you have referred to, and this can be seen from the minutes in Dobanovci, also in the preparations for the adoption of the various plans, the Vance Owen and the contact group plans. But I said that obviously that influence was not sufficient since they did not accept those plans. So I think that a part of the leadership of Republika Srpska had a different aspiration, and that was for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to be drawn into the war at all costs, and I think there was a joint meeting of the Assembly of Republika Srpska and the Serbian Krajina at Plitvice in response to our pressure to accept the contact group plan, and they wanted to create some kind of a joint Serbian Republic between these two entities which absolutely none of us could accept, you in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that connection, as a jigsaw is being formed using the wrong pieces, Mr. Nice asked you whether the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs came to the building where my offices were, that is, the presidency of Serbia. You said yes, but you added that most frequently, this occurred prior to negotiations. There were many negotiations which were most frequently conducted in Geneva. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I assume that you know on the basis of those negotiations which were not secret and which were led first by Vance and Owen, and after that by Owen and Stoltenberg, that the efforts of the Republic of Serbia and me personally were geared towards the achievement of a peaceful solution. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice asked you about Mladic. You said that he was unpredictable, and that between us, and this doesn't apply only to Mladic, but to the -- to several members of the leadership, that relations deteriorated after the Vance Owen plan was not accepted. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the financing of the budget of Yugoslavia, that while you were the president, Serbia's share in the budget was 95 per cent, that is, its financing of the budget was 95 per cent, and that later on it was even higher?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that show that Serbia, within the limits of its possibilities and under very difficult economic conditions actually bore the full burden of financing the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely true. There can be no doubt about that. And I must add that that item in the budget devoted to the Army of Yugoslavia, because of the overall economic conditions was never fulfilled as planned, so that the Army of Yugoslavia was constantly facing financial problems, had to contend with those problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the election to various posts in the general staff, and I'm not speaking about my own personal role, but our common position was that these should be people who opted for Yugoslavia, who were Yugoslavia-oriented, and that those people were selected and promoted and that that was our policy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Nice went on to ask you in -- about the alleged militarisation of the police, and then you answered that it was not right to say that the police had been militarised. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation why every effort it being made to impose -- to give the impression that the police was militarised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's no need for me to present any assumptions on my part. I say, and I stand by what I said, that this -- at least as regards the Republic of Serbia, the police was given priority over the army of Yugoslavia. As to your question, it would be difficult for me to comment on it. I could only give you my assumptions, and I don't think that would be in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The police that was first called Milicija, and then Policija, was within the competence of Serbia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of it within the competence of Serbia, and a part of it within the competence of the federal government. Until October or November, 1992, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What the authorities of Serbia were involved in, had to do with the police of Serbia. As for Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia covered 95 per cent of the budget of Yugoslavia. So when it came to the competencies of Yugoslavia, Serbia was the one who carried out its obligations in good faith, assisting in every respect it could and contributing in such a high percentage. He asked you in connection with the ranks of police, in a context to the effect that military ranks were applied to the police. First, is it clear that ranks in the police were not military ranks, but police ranks, and that a major or a captain or a general in the police was no military major or captain or general, but a police major, captain, or general. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way. I spoke about the dissatisfaction in answer to a question that the dissatisfaction this provoked within the top echelons of the general staff of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was not their affair, that is my first comment. And secondly, did that in any way jeopardise their own status or position? Did that interfere with the army in any way whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the standpoint of ranks, certainly not, though comparisons were made, and I think that only France has police ranks in addition to us. Of course, this needn't mean anything, that is, they have military ranks in the police, in the gendarmerie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: An attempt has been made here, and there was a man who, I never heard of such an occupation policeologist, he was explaining that the law on ranks had a special purpose. Do you believe that that law on ranks had any special purpose except to put some order in the police? Did I have any bad intentions, any secret agenda by using ranks in the police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday, and let me repeat today, that general ranks or ranks that were introduced in the police did not represent any proof showing that that was the militarisation of the police. I said something else, and I assume you remember that very well, that I personally thought that you did so as a concession to Mr. Radovan Stojicic that was -- rather than being it necessary. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. I thought you explained that Radovan Stojicic did not have the necessary qualifications for the post he held.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, for the post, he certainly had the necessary qualifications. But I compared the rank of colonel general in the understanding of the general staff of the army of Yugoslavia at the time and the rank of colonel general in the army of Yugoslavia. And I said that for the rank of general as such in the army of Yugoslavia, you need to have at least a Ph.D., to have graduated from the National Defence School, very high marks for command duties, and then I compared that with the activities of Radovan Stojicic on condition that we treat those ranks on an equal footing. If they are not on an equal footing, then my comparison is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume you will admit that you cannot compare something that exists for decades and centuries as a method of work, as a procedure of promotion in the military and when something new is being introduced in the police. And something that has a tradition, when it is something new, can have no tradition behind it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, but you know that I personally, by my own nature and by my own orientation, because of family history, for many years in the past I was more on the side of the army and was against the introduction of these ranks in the police, especially as they were introduced only in the public security and not in the state security, who were left without those ranks. Of course, when I say this, I have no ulterior motive, and I'm not saying that anything was being done, prompted by such motives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this referred to the uniform part of the police. The state security is not a uniformed section of the police, so there was no need to introduce ranks. According to the vertical chain of responsibility, all officials in the ministry, from the highest to the lowest, had their superiors and, in the final analysis, were accountable to the Minister of Internal Affairs. Is that right? And to whom was he accountable to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Minister of Internal Affairs is accountable to the president of the republican government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The government in the first place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were asked about Zoran Sokolovic, and he held the highest political positions, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He used to be secretary of the central committee, he was president of the National Assembly. After that, he was Minister of Internal Affairs. He was a very dedicated, and in every sense of the word, a man of firm convictions in the leadership of the Socialist Party of Serbia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, as a civilian and as a politician, as a Minister of the Police, he had no rank. He had no general or any other rank. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't have any such rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explain, then, please, as I didn't quite understand what you meant when you said that he didn't have real power. Did he perform his duties, or did he not perform his duties?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He performed the position of Minister of the Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Minister of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it was called then, and then later I think he was still a minister when it became the Ministry of the Police or whatever it was that changed after ranks were given and everything that followed. But I don't think that is important. Anyway, I am convinced on the basis of the knowledge I have, that as regards public security, the main moves were made in the first place by Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he headed the public security services just as Stanisic headed the state security. So Stojicic led the public and Stanisic the state security service. Do you know that if they had a problem, or if they wanted to talk to me, they would come, all of them, all three would come. The minister and the heads of two different departments, all three of them together.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in that context that I said that Sokolovic didn't have real power. What I meant was that all three came to see you whenever they had a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, that throws a completely different light on all this, but my impression was, and probably no one could refute this who was familiar with those relationships, that both Stojicic and Stanisic had a great deal of respect for Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so, as opposed to the minister who took over afterwards. That is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the fact that the military security for a period of time was excluded from the possibility of intercepting and tapping into telephone conversations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that this took place when the federal state service security no longer existed, when there was only the republican security service that was in existence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is this: I know that of the whole events that led up to eliminating the security administration and department of the army of Yugoslavia to tap into telephone conversations and control them, and that decision was taken - now I'm presenting the assumption here that it was General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic, the head of the security department of the army of Yugoslavia, and this decision was made in 1993, which means that the federal state security service did not exist at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, not at that time. Now, when it comes to republican state security, because it was guaranteed by the constitution, the inviolability of telephone conversations and the right to communicate, et cetera, letters, and so on, there was a provision that authorisation could be given if it was signed by the president of the supreme court, and only on that basis.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, they met every Monday, that is the head of state security of Serbia and the Supreme Court judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that they met every Monday, but I do know about that particular provision stipulating what it did, so I believe that what Stanisic told me is true and correct, that no measure was ever applied without a signature from the president of the Supreme Court. So as we're talking about the Supreme Court of Serbia, and as we're talking about the security service of Serbia, and as we're talking about every decree that had to be signed by the Supreme Court, I personally, and now I'm asking you whether you are aware and have knowledge of, this but I was personally informed that the military security service, if there are military security reasons to introduce a measure to that effect, which had to pass through this procedure because all the citizens were equal before the law, it was never refused by the State Security Service of Serbia for individuals for which the military security service was in charge and the request came from the military security service. So it was never refused, and this kind of procedure was always put into practice. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite possibly it was like that. I don't know whether that was actually the way it was. But they did ask me to ask you for that, and you will remember that we discussed it several times, that the security service be returned that right to be able to tap into conversations. And even with the pretext in respect to what you just said, that they don't always have to inform the State Security Service of everything they learn, all the intelligence gained on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, without informing the supreme court, this wouldn't have been possible for the army either in view of the provisions that held true, but there is --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the supreme military court, too, and I think that later on everything was returned to the state of affairs it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was returned to that situation, state of affairs unlawfully and illegally, but let that remain my own personal opinion on that subject. Now, you were asked by Mr. Nice whether the accused had control over high-ranking officers of the JNA. Your answer wasn't quite clear to me. Did I have control of some high-ranking JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeated the same thing and said that the word "control" was too strong a term, but I said that you were closer to some generals than you were to others. But that is a relative assessment. That's as it may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's all right, Mr. Lilic. Now, I'm sure you will remember that I was very busy with all the work I had, and -- but I was deprived of all possibilities of dealing with the army as such, and that, in fact, I didn't deal in army matters at all except for taking part in the Supreme Defence Council meetings which I had to do pursuant to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to give you an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but let me just remind you of a conversation you and I had. I'm sure you will remember and won't deny it. You asked me, you said, "You have a lot of obligations and lots of things to do. Can I be of assistance." And I said to you, "What you have under the constitutional competencies, that is to say the army, you deal with that. Because I really don't have time to devote myself, even the least bit of time to that area except that I will come to any meetings when they are convened."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was a lucky force of circumstance, that the army was retained, that it remained the cohesive factor in safeguarding Yugoslavia and preserving Yugoslavia because I think on the internal political plane it did show a great deal of understanding for internal policy. We were talking about certain people here from times before 1993, that is to say, some people who stayed on in the army in 1994 and who were closer to the police, if I can use the term, what I meant was Bozo Stevanovic, Boro Ivanovic, and some others. So in that context, was the answer. That is to say, that you had -- you felt closer towards some of them than others. You liked more -- some more than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said maybe. Yes, well maybe I did meet them on different ceremonial occasions, some of the other generals. But you mentioned yesterday General Marijanovic, for example. I heard of him first he was put forward by General Ojdanic, the new chief of staff of the general staff to a post in the general staff. As for General Boro Ivanovic, I didn't know him personally at all. Ojdanic, I did know him by sight, I would see him around, and I gained the impression that he was a very good man, a very honourable and honest man. And at the time, I didn't know that he was a very well-educated man and a very clever man, too. I don't know if you share my views on that. As for Bozo Stevanovic, yes, that's true, he did come to see me. He came to complain, in fact, and he was angry with me because I didn't use my influence and bring it to bear for him to be appointed chief of the general staff because he was one of the candidates put forward at the time. But I do not know that I had close contacts with any of the generals, not a single general, in fact, from the JNA or army of Yugoslavia. And I can say that I perhaps knew Kadijevic best. He was federal secretary at the time, and I knew him, of course, on a professional basis in terms of the post he occupied?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer all this. Can you deal with any of this, Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, I can, Mr. May, yes. As you brought up the name of General Marijanovic, I'm sure you had heard about him, if not seen him beforehand, when General Ojdanic was the commander of the 1st Army, which as you know very well took up over 50 per cent of the area of responsibility of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, 50 per cent. Marijanovic was the chief of staff, and I think that he followed the Uzice Corps. I know that both of them worked in tandem, if I can say that. But I think you also know him from the days of the negotiations and signing of the Manovo [phoen] agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was in Ojdanic was in the general staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've stopped you because you've interrupted the witness. You spoke for about 5 minutes yourself, and then expect him to answer in a minute, it is absurd. Yes, Mr. Lilic, is there something else you want to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just with respect to General Ivanovic, that was a very specific case with respect to the relationship of the general staff the army of Yugoslavia. I think this took place in the space of 1992, 1993, and 1994, in the course of those particular years, and I might have mentioned him in the context of saying that the military and court supported him. And as far as Mr. Stevanovic was concerned, he was promised that he would be chief of the general staff, or at least was a candidate for that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a convenient time to adjourn. What we have in mind is this, that, Mr. Milosevic, you should have the first two sessions tomorrow afternoon -- tomorrow morning. That will give you an hour or so more than the Prosecution have had. And it would also leave an hour for the amicus and any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I have to protest against that decision because it was quite obvious that Mr. Nice was skimming over the documents, riding over them, and now you're giving me the same amount of time that Mr. Nice had. And I cannot ride over all these documents as he did to introduce them as exhibits, to say to the witness is this an authentic document, have it exhibited and so on and so forth. I think that this is extremely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in mind. The proposal was that you would have an hour more than the Prosecution, not the same time. So. We will review the position. I've said that. Mr. Nice, it may become necessary, it will not be possible tomorrow to sit beyond the usual time. It's not possible to extend the hours today for one reason: Apparently the accused becomes deprived of all exercise if we go beyond the time. Now, we're looking into that, to see whether that's right or not. But the upshot is that we can't sit beyond the usual time. It may become necessary for the witness to return at some stage if we can't finish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we, Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that's necessary, then I'm sure that can be achieved. This is a witness which I shall wish to have a modest amount of time in re-examination, the nature of the evidence he's given, the position he occupies and so on, is such that some re-examination is inevitably essential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be sensible to have some discussion with the witness which, of course, you have permission to see when he could come back, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll deal with that. We can best deal with that via his lawyer, I think might be preferable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, whichever way you proceed is possible. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, yesterday, I asked you to give me much more time than Mr. Nice had, precisely for the reasons I explained. I don't personally think that the witness will refuse to extend his time for cross-examination after the weekend. I'm sure he'll be available, and I don't see why he shouldn't be. And why the most important thing is to finish everything by the end of business tomorrow? If we're talking about such a large pile of documents, and I cannot skim through the documents in the way that Mr. Nice did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness may or may not be able to come back. We have to some regard to his convenience. But if necessary, we will ask him to do so at some time which is suitable. We, of course, have in mind the time, but time must be used to the best advantage by everybody here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other point, a number of next week's witnesses I think are scheduled for particular dates and have had difficulty finding dates convenient to them in one or two cases because they have been fixed or times when the accused has been unable to attend for reasons outside his control. Second point is, I'd ask the Chamber to have in mind the character of some of this morning's cross-examination, which was reading out very large passages of meetings to the witness and asking very limited questions. It's a matter for the accused, but of course documents that relate accounts of meetings, and this is going to occur much more when we eventually get the documents of the SDC meetings, are substantially documents that do speak for themselves. They may have to be produced by some technique, but once they're in, they're in, and that's why my questions have always been pointed and less time has been taken by pointed questions than by simply going through the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have that in mind. But this is an area in which the fact that an accused is representing himself must be borne in mind, not represented by professional lawyers who might be able to do the things more expeditiously. Yes, we'll adjourn until tomorrow. Mr. Lilic, would you please be back at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.56 p.m. to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of June, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
